record.body:
The commands below work once the npm packages and the matching GitHub release are published (see [Maintainer release steps](#maintainer-release-steps)). Node.js 22+ and npm are required; end users do not need Rust or Docker.

## Create an app

After publication:

```sh
npm create typedpress@0.3.0 my-app
cd my-app
npm run dev
```

The creator installs the matching `typedpress` version and TypeScript. The compiler package downloads the exact version for your operating system and CPU and verifies the archive's SHA-256. `typedpress dev` uses pinned WordPress Studio CLI 2.2.0 to supply native PHP, WordPress and SQLite.

Open `/index.html` on the WordPress URL printed in the terminal: the project's `public/` folder is served at the site root. Your public frontend, API, login and native WordPress admin share that origin. WordPress's theme retains its homepage. Add a note through “Write a note”; the example permits public reads and restricts writes to WordPress editors. Use the local admin credentials printed by TypedPress only for development.

Edit `public/` for the frontend and `typedpress.config.ts` for the backend. TypedPress watches both. Refresh to see changes. The generated client in `tp/_generated/client/` is ready for a TypeScript frontend, and `client.ts` demonstrates its types. A frontend framework is optional. Backend TypeScript compiles to PHP; unsupported language/library behavior fails compiler checks rather than becoming a Node.js service.

```sh
npm run check
npm run typecheck
npm run build
npm run dev -- --port 9123
npm run wp -- core version
npm run stop
```

Stopping preserves your local SQLite content. Commit generated migrations and client files; keep `.tp/`, dependencies and secrets out of Git. The emitted deployment artifact is `tp/dist/wp-content`, not the local Studio database. Production provisioning and data migration require the deployment lifecycle for your target WordPress site.

Use `npm create typedpress@0.3.0 my-app -- --no-install` to scaffold without installing dependencies. Choose a new directory: existing empty directories, populated directories and symbolic links are all refused. An installation failure preserves the newly created app for a retry.

## Install the command separately

After publication:

```sh
npm install --global typedpress@0.3.0
typedpress --help
```

Prebuilt targets are macOS arm64/x64 and glibc 2.39+ Linux arm64/x64 (Ubuntu 24.04 or newer). Windows, older glibc and musl Linux need a compiler you provide. There is no automatic Cargo build or search for another `typedpress` executable.

| Setting                                               | Effect                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `TP_BIN=/absolute/path/to/typedpress`                 | Use your explicitly provided executable, without downloading. Relative paths and missing/non-executable files fail.              |
| `TP_CACHE_DIR=/absolute/cache`                        | Store version/target-specific compiler downloads here. The default is `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/tp/npm`, or `~/.cache/tp/npm`.            |
| `TP_OFFLINE=1`                                        | Use only the verified cache or `TP_BIN`. A missing cached version fails with a next step.                                        |
| `TP_RELEASE_BASE_URL=https://mirror/releases/v0.3.0/` | Read the exact archive and checksum from a release mirror. `file://` and loopback HTTP are supported for local maintainer tests. |

Every release needs `typedpress-vVERSION-RUST_TARGET.tar.gz` and its `.sha256` file. The checksum file contains the lowercase SHA-256, two spaces and the exact archive basename. Downloads fail clearly if either asset is missing, malformed or corrupt. Cached executables are checked against their installation receipt before reuse. SHA-256 establishes integrity of the downloaded archive; it is not a publisher signature.

## Homebrew

The workflow generates `homebrew/Formula/typedpress.rb` from all four real archives after verifying each checksum. It never substitutes placeholder hashes. Maintainers must publish those exact archives and create or select a public tap before advertising a `brew install` command.

The formula installs the executable and original license notices, depends on Homebrew Node, and checks a real TypedPress config in `brew test`. Node supplies npm for `typedpress dev`. macOS signing and notarization are deferred to the signing team; the current archives explicitly declare themselves unsigned. No signing bypass is installed.

## Maintainer release steps

The repository publishes four npm packages: `typedpress` and `create-typedpress` (the Cargo
version, 0.3.0 today) and the independently versioned `@typedpress/astro` and
`@typedpress/blocks` (0.1.0). `CONTRIBUTING.md` describes the release workflow.

1. Make sure the npm account that publishes owns the unscoped names `typedpress` and
   `create-typedpress` (both unpublished) and the `@typedpress` scope. Do not overwrite the
   older `@spacefast/zero` package.
1. For a compiler release, set one new version in root `Cargo.toml` and both CLI package
   manifests; `node scripts/release/version.mjs VERSION` rejects mismatches. Merge it, then push
   an immutable `vVERSION` tag on that commit.
1. The tag runs the release workflow. It builds seven native archives and `typedpress.wasm`,
   smoke-checks each binary, packs and content-checks all four npm packages, installs the packed
   CLI from the archives, runs the packed starter end to end, generates the Homebrew formula and
   attaches the archives, `.sha256` files, wasm, `compiler-assets.json`, the exact source archive
   and the four npm tarballs to the GitHub release. The release assets must be publicly
   downloadable (the repository public) before the npm launcher can install anonymously.
1. Check the published release from a machine without GitHub credentials:
   `TP_CACHE_DIR=$(mktemp -d) npx --yes ./typedpress-VERSION.tgz --version` and `check` on an
   example. Have the signing team sign/notarize payloads when ready, then regenerate archive
   checksums and the formula from the final bytes. Never reuse pre-signing hashes.
1. Publish the tarballs attached to the release, in this order:
   `npm publish typedpress-VERSION.tgz`, then `create-typedpress-VERSION.tgz`, then
   `typedpress-astro-0.1.0.tgz` and `typedpress-blocks-0.1.0.tgz` (scoped packages publish public
   through their `publishConfig`). Do not rerun `npm pack` from installed tarballs: the prepack
   scripts run from the source repository.
1. Copy the generated formula to the chosen public tap's `Formula/typedpress.rb`, run
   `brew install` and `brew test typedpress` on supported machines, then publish the tap commit.
   Verify the public npm create command before announcing it.

### Test an unpublished release locally

Use a private target directory and a new evidence directory. No command below publishes anything.

```sh
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/typedpress-setup-target cargo build --release --locked
TP_SETUP_BINARY=/tmp/typedpress-setup-target/release/typedpress \
  TP_SETUP_EVIDENCE=/tmp/typedpress-framework-setup-local-test \
  node scripts/release/acceptance.mjs
```

The acceptance run creates a local archive and real checksum, packs and installs both npm packages into clean temporary projects, scaffolds with automatic dependency installation, checks generated client types, runs `npm run dev` on an available port, reads content created through native WordPress, and stops/deletes only its own site. Studio configuration, daemon, caches and SQLite files are isolated. Evidence and the scaffold remain under the requested `/tmp` directory; the disposable WordPress data is removed. This proves local Linux behavior when run on Linux; it does not prove macOS, arm64, public release delivery, Homebrew installation or signing.

For manual packaging, `node scripts/release/archive.mjs BINARY RUST_TARGET OUTPUT SOURCE_COMMIT` requires matching HEAD and committed compiler/runtime sources. `--working-tree` explicitly marks a local test artifact whose revision is only the base commit. `node scripts/release/homebrew.mjs OUTPUT NEW_FORMULA_PATH` requires all four real matching archives. Never publish local test artifacts labelled `local-working-tree-test`.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.description: What these docs cover and where to start.

record.body:
TypedPress compiles TypeScript into a WordPress plugin. You describe your data, your server functions and your pages; WordPress stores the content, runs the editor and sign-in, and serves the site. No JavaScript runs on the server.

These docs are the longer reference. Two shorter ways in:

- [The guide](/) is one page that shows every feature with an example.
- [The playground](/play) builds an app in your browser as you type, and runs it in WordPress.

## Names

The framework is being renamed from TypedPress to TypedPress. The code today still uses the First names, and so do these docs: `typedpress.config.ts`, the `tp/` folder, the `typedpress` command. The guide lists what each name becomes.

## How these docs are made

Each page here is a Markdown file in `content/docs/` of this site's repository. The site is a TypedPress app: `typedpress sync` stores each file as a WordPress item, and one page, `tp/app/docs/[...path]/page.tsx`, renders them all with the navigation on the left and the headings on the right.

```ts title="tp/schema.ts"
export const docs = collection({
  title: text(),
  slug: slug({ source: "title" }),
  content: richText().optional(),
  description: text().optional(),
}, { hierarchical: true, url: "/docs/:path", sync: "content/docs/**/*.md" });
```

An editor can change a doc in WordPress, and `typedpress sync` writes the change back to the file.

record.body:
TypedPress Admin is the default admin of every TypedPress app. `typedpress build` puts the
`typedpress-admin` plugin (compiled assets included) into the artifact next to
`typedpress-runtime` and `typedpress-app-<name>`; activate it after the app. It runs at
`/wp-admin/new/`, the address the upstream admin used, and classic
`/wp-admin/` stays complete and unchanged beside it. A subdirectory installation
uses its own prefix, for example `/blog/wp-admin/new/`.

```ts
import { collection, defineConfig, richText, text } from "typedpress";

const posts = collection({
  title: text(),
  body: richText().optional(),
  summary: text().optional(),
}, {
  title: "title",
  content: "body",
  access: { read: "anyone", create: "editor", update: "editor", delete: "admin" },
});

// No setting needed: TypedPress Admin ships. `admin: false` leaves only classic wp-admin.
export default defineConfig({ name: "my-app", collections: { posts } });
```

Use your normal WordPress account. WordPress owns authentication, capabilities,
REST nonces, users, settings, plugins, themes, media and the block editor.

### Addresses

| URL                                                   | What it serves                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `/wp-admin/new/<route>`                               | TypedPress Admin. Apache rewrites it to `wp-admin/admin.php?page=typedpress-admin`; the route stays in the path.                                                            |
| `/wp-admin/admin.php?page=typedpress-admin&p=<route>` | The same page on any server. A server that does not read `.htaccess` (nginx, and WordPress Studio's server behind `typedpress dev`) redirects `/wp-admin/new/<route>` here. |
| `/wp-admin/`                                          | Classic wp-admin, unchanged. Its `TypedPress` menu entry opens TypedPress Admin.                                                                                            |
| `/typedpress-admin/<route>`                           | The earlier address: a permanent redirect to `/wp-admin/new/<route>`.                                                                                                       |

The page is a wp-admin page: `admin.php` signs the visitor in (`auth_redirect`)
and builds wp-admin's menus, so plugin menu entries appear in TypedPress Admin's
sidebar. The plugin writes its rule into `.htaccess` on the first web request
after it is activated or updated (WP-CLI never writes that file).

After signing in, WordPress's default destination (`/wp-admin/`) becomes
`/wp-admin/new/`. A page the visitor asked for (`redirect_to`) is kept.
`Classic admin` in TypedPress Admin's sidebar and command palette opens
`/wp-admin/`; `TypedPress` in wp-admin's menu returns. Existing plugin settings and
classic plugin screens remain accessible in both.

`admin: false` in `defineConfig` leaves the plugin out of the build, and a build
that adds it removes the plugin from the output. Classic wp-admin is then the
only admin and login lands there, as in WordPress.

Editor asset URLs use WordPress's registered installation URL, including the
subdirectory prefix.

## Screens in both admins

A screen declared once with `tp_admin_register_screen()` appears in TypedPress
Admin (`/wp-admin/new/screens/<id>`) and as a classic wp-admin page, rendered by
the same component, with actions that run Abilities. TypedPress declares Schema
versions and one list per `table()` kind this way. See
admin-screens.md.

## Source scope

The admin includes the complete distributable next-admin / CIAB Admin plugin
package, route, field, dashboard-widget and PHP library trees. This includes
Dashboard, native Posts and Pages, Users, Plugins, Themes, Settings, Design,
Styles, Navigation, taxonomy and comment fields, importers and the AI-agent
integration package. These surfaces are retained alongside TypedPress's schema-driven
collections, tables, relations, media and globals.

The home route `/` is the upstream dashboard, as upstream has it;
`/collections` is TypedPress's collection overview (Collections → All collections in
the sidebar). The sidebar includes native WordPress content types as well
as TypedPress collections; mapped types appear through the access-aware TypedPress adapter.
Native content uses WordPress's editor routes. The complete upstream attachment
editor is at `/types/attachment/edit/:id`; `Edit image` opens it from TypedPress
media details, with crop/rotate/flip tools and WordPress-native image saving. TypedPress content uses the same block
editor with Secure Custom Fields and TypedPress's existing REST authorization.
Database tables use TypedPress's table forms and relation pickers. Hiding navigation
never grants or revokes access: the server remains the authority.

## Styles

TypedPress Admin keeps the upstream look. Where a pinned WordPress package changed
underneath it, the change is the smallest one that keeps that look:

| Change                                                                                                                     | Why                                                                                                               |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `font-weight: var(--wpds-typography-font-weight-emphasis, 499)` (and `-default, 400`) for `$font-weight-medium`/`-regular` | the pinned `@wordpress/base-styles` removed those variables; the tokens carry the same values                     |
| Color settings name the background seed `background` and use `@wordpress/theme` directly                                   | upstream's `@typedpress-admin/theme` shim passed the old `bg` seed; WordPress 7.1's `wp-theme` reads `background` |
| The site hub wraps its title in a `<span>`                                                                                 | the upstream stylesheet sizes the link's first span, which the pinned `@wordpress/ui` Link no longer adds         |
| `style` on design-system popups and primitives                                                                             | the pinned Base UI types moved it                                                                                 |
| The page opts in to view transitions (`@view-transition`)                                                                  | the router starts one on each navigation; without the opt-in the browser aborts it with an error                  |

Everything else that differs from the retained originals is behaviour: the
mount and subdirectory URLs, TypedPress's schema screens, and the AI chat button,
which needs a provider (see External services). TypedPress's own screens
(`packages/schema`) use `@wordpress/components` and DataViews with upstream's
spacing.

## WordPress packages instead of copies

Where the WordPress floor (7.1) allows it, TypedPress Admin uses WordPress's own
packages instead of the copies the upstream admin carried:

| Was                                                                         | Now                | How it loads                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `packages/theme` (`@typedpress-admin/theme`)                                | `@wordpress/theme` | WordPress 7.1's `wp-theme` script; `useThemeProviderStyles` is its private API, unlocked as core's packages do. WordPress 7.1 marks that private API deprecated (removal planned for 7.3), so the AI panel and the editor settings need a replacement before TypedPress supports 7.3 |
| `packages/views`: `useView`, `loadView`, the view types and preference keys | `@wordpress/views` | bundled into the admin (WordPress 7.1 has no `wp-views` script)                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `packages/views`: `useViewConfig`, the `DataViews` layout wrapper           | stays TypedPress's | `useViewConfig` reads TypedPress Admin's own fields (tabs, quick and add forms, labels, actions) from `/typedpress-admin/v1/view-config`, which core's endpoint doesn't serve                                                                                                        |
| `packages/wp-build`                                                         | stays for now      | `@wordpress/build` targets WordPress core's admin boot and a newer `@wordpress/theme` than 7.1 ships; it moves with TypedPress Admin onto core's boot                                                                                                                                |

The packages are pinned with the rest in `apps/pnpm-workspace.yaml`. Their former
copies stay recorded in `upstream-inventory.json`, with each retained input.

### Saved list layouts reset once

`@wordpress/views` stores a user's list layout (columns, sort, layout type,
page size) under `dataviews-<kind>-<name>-<tab>` where the copy used
`<kind>-<name>`, and it saves only what the user changed from the default.
Layouts saved before this change are not read: every list opens on its default
layout once, then saves under the new key. Nothing is migrated.

The six lists that change, and how:

| List                                  | Route                                 | What changes                                                                        |
|---------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Users                                 | `/users`, `/users/list/<role>`        | each role tab keeps its own layout; the role filter is the tab's and is never saved |
| Posts and pages (each post type)      | `/types/<type>/list/<tab>`            | each status tab keeps its own layout; the tab's status filter is never saved        |
| Plugins                               | `/plugins/list/<tab>`                 | each tab (all, active, inactive, …) keeps its own layout                          |
| Categories, tags and other taxonomies | `/types/<type>/taxonomies/<taxonomy>` | layout saved under `all`                                                            |
| Themes                                | `/design/themes`                      | layout saved under `all`                                                            |
| Navigation menus                      | `/design/navigation/list`             | layout saved under `all`                                                            |

Changing a column and changing it back now removes the saved layout rather than
saving a copy of the default. A tab's filters (a role, a status) are applied on
top of whatever the user saved, so a saved filter on the same field can't
override the tab.

## Provenance and updates

The input distribution declares GPL-2.0-or-later. Its archive contains no Git
metadata, so an upstream Git revision could not be verified. The exact input is
recorded in `runtime/admin/upstream-inventory.json`: each original path and
SHA-256, its destination, and the adapter disposition. The input digest is:

```text
06b2a01779baec3292803ad57704981703e4f0783230097746baeb67f456e8cf
```

This digest covers the 1,094 distributable plugin source files; repository agent
instruction files are excluded. It identifies the archive, not a Git commit.
Upstream root configuration/bootstrap and PHP tests are retained under
`upstream-metadata/` as reference material, outside the active plugin loader; `typedpress build` leaves
that folder out of the plugin, as it leaves out the JS workspace `apps/`.
For each adapted file, `upstream-metadata/adapter-originals/` retains its complete
input after namespace and privacy normalization. `retainedSourcePath` and
`normalizedSha256` identify that copy; unchanged inputs point to their active
file. This includes the original image-edit backport: the active attachment
controller uses WordPress's current native implementation instead.
Private tracker links and service references in documentation are redacted.
Dependency packages retain their original notices. The generated
`build/THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.txt` includes bundled dependency licenses and every
workspace notice.

Local changes use `@typedpress-admin/*` and `tp_admin_*` names, the existing TypedPress
mount/login/iframe adapter, a schema bridge, native menu merging, widget
registration and compatibility adjustments for the pinned WordPress packages.
The package tree remains intact. Review `adaptedSha256` and `adaptation` in the
inventory before rebasing an upstream file; a matching original hash identifies
an unchanged input. Replace source and rebuild the complete workspace together.

## Build and verification

Use Node 22 or later and pnpm 10.16.0. WordPress dependencies are pinned to one
snapshot in `apps/pnpm-workspace.yaml`; the lockfile pins transitive packages.
Build in a private copy when another worker uses the checkout:

```sh
cd runtime/admin/apps
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm build
pnpm typecheck
pnpm exec jest --runInBand
```

From the repository root, `node --test tests/wp/admin/upstream-drift.test.mjs`
checks every retained input and active adapter against the generated inventory.

`pnpm build` writes the full module registry, route/field/widget registrations,
assets, license bundle and source manifest to `../build`. Commit source and
compiled output together. `php tests/php/vendor_drift.php` checks the committed
admin source digest and license inventory, alongside the repository's other
vendor guards. Two builds from identical inputs must produce identical files.

The existing browser owner is `apps/wp-journey/admin.spec.ts`. Against a
disposable WordPress artifact created by `tests/wp/harness.sh`, run:

```sh
cd runtime/admin/apps
pnpm exec playwright install chromium
TP_WP_HARNESS=/path/to/disposable-harness.json \
pnpm exec playwright test --config wp-journey/playwright.config.ts
```

Those journeys execute real WordPress/SCF saves, publish and anonymous reads,
table relations, media upload/edit/delete, role restrictions, native settings,
users/plugins/themes/design/editor routes and classic navigation. The upstream
PHPUnit sources are retained as reference; their original monorepo bootstrap
requires fixtures outside this plugin and is not the standalone test runner.
The pre-existing Jest exclusion for the pinned design-system tabs primitive is
unchanged; it remains a known verification gap.

## External services and examples

The AI-agent package includes its context store, abilities lifecycle, cache
invalidation and provider slot. It includes no AI service. A WordPress plugin
may enable `ai_agent_enabled` through `tp_admin_boot_context` and implement
`window.wpOrchestratorAgent.ask`. Missing providers reject requests explicitly.
See the package README for its events and slot contract. Hosted AI execution
and hosted account invitations are not proven by local WordPress tests.

The slot stays unwired on purpose. It needs a model that turns a prompt into
answers and tool calls; TypedPress's agent surface (the site's MCP endpoint,
`/wp-json/mcp/typedpress-<app>`, and the app's Abilities) is the tools side of that,
not a model. Wiring the two together would still need a hosted model and its
credentials, which TypedPress does not ship. An agent outside the site (Claude Code,
an MCP client) already uses that endpoint and the same Abilities the admin's
screens run, under the same permissions; see `typedpress mcp` and docs/agents.md.

Telemetry calls use an inert compatibility adapter: TypedPress sends no upstream
usage events. The three upstream dashboard demonstration widgets retain their
example data and explicitly label it as such. They do not report live traffic,
weather or recent posts. Native plugin/theme catalog installation, update,
mail delivery, external AI providers and publishing services need their own live
provider verification; rendering their routes does not establish those effects.

fields.title: Agents
fields.description: How agents use an app: abilities, MCP and the Markdown twin of every page.

record.body:
An agent meets a TypedPress project in two places: while the project is being
written, and when the app runs. TypedPress has an MCP server for each:

|                 | Development time                                                                                        | Runtime                                              |
|-----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| What it is      | `typedpress mcp`, in the `typedpress` binary                                                            | the site's endpoint, `/wp-json/mcp/typedpress-<app>` |
| Who uses it     | a coding agent working on the project's source                                                          | any agent using the app's data and actions           |
| Transport       | stdio                                                                                                   | Streamable HTTP                                      |
| What it answers | the project's schema, compiler diagnostics, TypedPress's documentation, the command table, the dev site | one tool per collection operation and action         |
| Access          | the local files, and the local dev site                                                                 | a WordPress user's access rules                      |

`typedpress init` sets the first one up in a project, with an `AGENTS.md` section and
the skills that carry the step-by-step procedures. This page is the reference
for both servers; the procedures are in the skills.

## Set a project up for coding agents: `typedpress init`

`typedpress init [dir]` writes what a coding agent needs into the project. A project
made with `npm create typedpress` already has them: the scaffolder runs
`typedpress init` once the compiler is installed.

| File                                    | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-----------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `AGENTS.md`                             | A section between `<!-- typedpress:begin -->` and `<!-- typedpress:end -->`: this project's kinds with their fields, access rules and API paths, its actions, jobs, pages and routes, the roles, the site's endpoints, every `typedpress` command, and the skills. |
| `.mcp.json`                             | A server named `typedpress` that starts `typedpress mcp` (below).                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `.agents/skills/`, `.claude/skills/`    | The skills this compiler carries, one per task (below).                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `.github/workflows/typedpress-sync.yml` | Only with `typedpress init --github`: the workflow that keeps synced content and the site in step through pull requests (Content in git). It is at the repository's root even when the project is in a folder of it.                                               |

The section is generated from the compiled project and from the command table,
so it describes this project, not TypedPress in general. Commit all of it.

The skills are in the layout of
[WordPress/agent-skills](https://github.com/WordPress/agent-skills): a
directory per skill with a `SKILL.md` whose front matter says when to use it.
Each is a short procedure that links to the documentation for depth:

| Skill                       | Task                                                                        |
|-----------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `typedpress-add-kind`       | Add a kind or a field, a `ref()`, an access rule; rename or remove a field. |
| `typedpress-write-action`   | Write an `action()` or a `job()`.                                           |
| `typedpress-add-page`       | Add a page, a layout or an HTTP route under `tp/app/`.                      |
| `typedpress-fix-diagnostic` | Read a compiler diagnostic and fix its cause.                               |
| `typedpress-dev-site`       | Run the local dev site and inspect it.                                      |
| `typedpress-connect-mcp`    | Connect an MCP client to a site's runtime endpoint.                         |
| `typedpress-migrate`        | Convert a Zero 0.8 app, or import another CMS's schema.                     |

- Text outside the two markers in `AGENTS.md` is yours. A rerun replaces the
  section and nothing else. A marker counts only on a line of its own, so prose
  that quotes one is left alone.
- A server already named `typedpress` in `.mcp.json`, and every other server, is
  left as it is. The entry is inserted into the file's text, so its formatting
  and numbers are unchanged.
- The skill files are TypedPress's: a rerun writes them back as this compiler has them.
  Delete `.claude/skills` or `.agents/skills` if you do not use that agent; a
  rerun does not bring it back.
- Files keep their permissions, and an `AGENTS.md` that links to another file of
  the project (`CLAUDE.md`) is written through the link. A skills directory that
  links outside the project is refused, before anything is written.
- The workflow is TypedPress's while its first line says `typedpress init --github` wrote it for this
  project: a rerun (with or without `--github`) writes it back when the synced folders change.
  Another project in the same repository leaves it alone. Delete that line to keep your own edits;
  it is never touched again.
- A project with its own `CLAUDE.md` should import the file with a line
  `@AGENTS.md`; `typedpress init` says so when it is missing.

When the config or the compiler changes, the files go out of date. `typedpress check`,
`typedpress build` and `typedpress dev` then print one line:

```text
hint: AGENTS.md and the agent skills no longer match this project or this compiler; run typedpress init to update them
```

Only a project that ran `typedpress init` gets the hint. In CI, `typedpress init --check`
writes nothing, names each file that would change, and exits 1 when there is one.

## Develop a project with a coding agent: `typedpress mcp`

`typedpress mcp [dir]` serves the project in `dir` (default: the current directory)
to a coding agent on stdin and stdout. `typedpress init` registers it in `.mcp.json`.
To register it by hand, for Claude Code, in the project's `.mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "typedpress": { "command": "npx", "args": ["--no-install", "typedpress", "mcp"] }
  }
}
```

For Codex: `codex mcp add first -- npx --no-install typedpress mcp`. `--no-install`
runs the `typedpress` the project already has from `typedpress` and never
downloads a package by that name. With a compiler built from source, use its
path in place of `npx --no-install typedpress`.

| Tool                       | What it returns                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|----------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `schema`                   | The project's kinds with their fields, access rules, relations and hooks; globals, actions, jobs, pages and HTTP routes, file buckets, roles, the Abilities the site registers, and the endpoints. `kind` narrows it to one kind.                                                 |
| `check`                    | The `typedpress-diagnostics` envelope `typedpress check --json` prints (compiler diagnostics). It writes nothing.                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `docs_search`, `docs_read` | TypedPress's documentation as built into this binary: the guides in `docs/` (not the design proposals or the pages for hosts and maintainers) and the docs site's pages. A long page or section read whole answers with its opening and its sections; pass `section` to read one. |
| `commands`                 | The command table `typedpress help` prints.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `dev_status`               | What `typedpress dev status --json` reports: whether the project has a local dev site, whether it runs, its URL and port, and whether a `typedpress dev` process is rebuilding it on save.                                                                                        |
| `query`                    | A kind's records from the local dev site, through `typedpress find`: `kind`, `where`, `orderBy`, `limit` (20 by default, at most 500), `offset`, `columns`, `with`. Like every request to the site, it first publishes scheduled posts that are due.                              |

`schema`, `check`, `docs_search` and `docs_read` compile or read from the
binary and need no site. `schema` and `check` read the files as they are at each
call, so an edit shows up without restarting the server. The same documentation
pages are also the server's resources, as `typedpress-docs:///<path>`.

`query` and the write tools run as the trusted command line, like `typedpress find`:
no access rules, drafts included. They are for a developer's own dev site:

- Without a flag, `query` reads this project's dev site and refuses any `site`.
  `typedpress mcp --allow-remote-read` lets it read another site, named as `--site`
  names one: a project directory, a deployment workspace or a WP-CLI `@alias`.
- The write tools are not listed without `--allow-writes`. With it, `run_action`,
  `insert` and `update` run `typedpress action`, `typedpress insert` and `typedpress update` on
  this project's dev site. They take no `site`, so they never reach another one.
- There is no delete tool.

A tool that runs a command (the compiler for `schema` and `check`, `typedpress find`
and the other site commands) stops it after 120 seconds, or the number of
seconds in `TP_MCP_TIMEOUT`, and stops it when the client cancels the request.

### Run the dev site from an agent

`typedpress dev` normally stays in the foreground until Ctrl+C, which an agent's
shell cannot do. Two things make it usable there:

- `typedpress dev --detach` returns once the site is up. The watcher keeps running
  in the background, rebuilds on save, and writes to `.tp/dev/dev.log`.
  `typedpress dev stop` stops it.
- Without the flag, `typedpress dev` does the same by itself when its output is not a
  terminal and one of `CLAUDECODE`, `CODEX_SANDBOX`, `AI_AGENT` or `AGENT` is
  set to something other than empty, `0` or `false`. It says so on stderr. It
  never does this when `CI` is set, and `--foreground` turns it off.

`typedpress dev status --json` (and the `dev_status` tool) answers from
`.tp/dev/state.json`, which `typedpress dev` writes when the site is up:

```json
{"state":"running","url":"http://localhost:8787","port":8787,"admin":"http://localhost:8787/wp-admin/","site":"/work/my-app/.tp/dev/wordpress","watching":true,"pid":41822,"log":"/work/my-app/.tp/dev/dev.log","wordpress":"7.2-beta5","php":"8.4"}
```

`state` is `none`, `stopped` or `running`, checked against the port itself.
`watching` is true while the recorded `typedpress dev` process exists; after
`--no-watch` it is false and `pid` is null. `typedpress dev status` without `--json`
still prints Studio's own report.

The server speaks MCP revision 2026-07-28 (no handshake; `server/discover`) and,
for clients that open with `initialize`, 2025-11-25 and 2025-06-18.

## Use the running app: the site's MCP endpoint

Connect an agent to the same data and actions your frontend uses. TypedPress registers
them with WordPress's core Abilities API. The required MCP Adapter plugin exposes
them through an app-specific Streamable HTTP server.

### Find the endpoint and tools

For `defineConfig({ name: "subscriptions", ... })`, connect to:

```text
https://your-site.example/wp-json/mcp/typedpress-subscriptions
```

Keep any WordPress subdirectory before `/wp-json`. The app name and resource
names become kebab-case. A config named `myTracker` uses `typedpress-my-tracker`.

The runtime registers each enabled collection or table operation, and each
action, as an ability. The adapter replaces the slash in an ability name with a
hyphen in its MCP tool name:

| Config operation                           | Core ability                         | MCP tool                             |
|--------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| `subscriptions.list(...)`                  | `subscriptions/subscriptions-list`   | `subscriptions-subscriptions-list`   |
| `subscriptions.get(id)`                    | `subscriptions/subscriptions-get`    | `subscriptions-subscriptions-get`    |
| `subscriptions.create(data)`               | `subscriptions/subscriptions-create` | `subscriptions-subscriptions-create` |
| `subscriptions.update(id, patch)`          | `subscriptions/subscriptions-update` | `subscriptions-subscriptions-update` |
| `subscriptions.delete(id)`                 | `subscriptions/subscriptions-delete` | `subscriptions-subscriptions-delete` |
| `actions.monthlyBurn({})`                  | `subscriptions/monthly-burn`         | `subscriptions-monthly-burn`         |
| `actions.renewingSoon({ days: 3 })`        | `subscriptions/renewing-soon`        | `subscriptions-renewing-soon`        |
| `actions.logCharge({ subscriptionId: 1 })` | `subscriptions/log-charge`           | `subscriptions-log-charge`           |
| `actions.cancel({ subscriptionId: 1 })`    | `subscriptions/cancel`               | `subscriptions-cancel`               |

`charges` and `categories` have the same operation suffixes. List tools accept
filters, ordering, pagination, and declared relation loads. Update takes
`{ "id": 1, "patch": { "notes": "Review before renewal" } }`. List results
wrap rows in `{ "rows": [...] }`; action results have the handler's shape.
Always inspect `tools/list` for the actual input schema before calling a tool.

A `collection()` also has one tool per step of its [staged version](/docs/guides/staged-versions):
`<kind>-stage`, `<kind>-staged-get`, `<kind>-staged-compare`,
`<kind>-staged-promote`, `<kind>-staged-discard` and `<kind>-staged-preview`.
An agent can stage a change to a published item, read the comparison, and
leave the promote to a person, or to a credential that is allowed that tool.
`table()` kinds, such as the ones in this app, have none.

`api: { delete: false }` removes that operation. `agents: false` keeps the
underlying ability registered for PHP and WP-CLI, while hiding it from public
ability REST discovery and the app's MCP server. Globals also expose get and
update abilities. Jobs are exposed only when explicitly opted in with
`agents: true`; the subscriptions reminder is not an agent tool.

The app server lists named tools directly. The adapter's separate default
server has discovery and execution meta-tools; it is not the app endpoint above.

The owning code is
`Register.php`, which calls
`wp_register_ability()` and the adapter's `create_server()`, and
`Invoke.php`, which routes execution
through the app pipeline. Input schemas come from
`JsonSchema.php`.
Abilities use the same access rules, field permissions, hooks, and transactions
as REST. An application password authenticates a WordPress user; it does not
bypass that user's access. In the subscriptions app, owner filters also apply
to MCP reads and writes. Trusted action handlers explicitly filter by owner.

### Who the agent is

The endpoint authenticates as core does. An agent connects as a WordPress user
with an application password, sent as HTTP Basic auth, and gets that user's
access and no more: the kinds' access rules, field permissions, hooks and
transactions apply to every tool call as they do on the API. An application
password is not the user's login password and not a TypedPress Identity browser token.

### Scoped agent credentials

`typedpress identity agent add <user> --name=<name>` creates an application password
for one agent. It is **read-only and has no access to personal data** until a
flag grants more:

| Flag                                 | Grants                                                                                                 |
|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--write`                            | creates, updates, deletes and abilities that aren't `readonly`                                         |
| `--personal`                         | reading and setting email fields and fields with a read rule, and reading a user's own account details |
| `--abilities=blog/posts-list,blog/*` | only these abilities; no other route but the app's schema                                              |

`typedpress identity agent list <user>`, `typedpress identity agent grant <user> <id>`
(with the same flags) and `typedpress identity agent revoke <user> <id>` manage them, and **Users → Profile →
Application Passwords** offers the same choices (*Allow writes*, *Allow personal
data*) and shows each password's scope.

A scope only narrows. The user's role, each kind's access rules and its field
rules still decide first, so a subscriber's credential with `--write` writes
what a subscriber may. It is enforced wherever the app can be reached: the
abilities run route, the MCP server, `/__tp/api/v1`, core's `/wp/v2` routes,
`/batch/v1` sub-requests, `?rest_route=` and method overrides. `GET /__tp/api/v1` reports the scope of the credential asking, under
`runtime.credential`.

Whatever its grants and its user's role, a scoped credential can't do the
things that would remove its own limits:

- read or change application passwords, so it can't widen itself or mint another;
- change the account it signs in as: its password, email, login, roles or
  sign-in methods (TypedPress Identity's and Two Factor's routes). With `--write --personal` it can still edit the rest of the profile;
- administer the site: plugins and themes (deactivating TypedPress would switch the
  scope off), site settings, creating or promoting users, and any other plugin's
  route that asks one of those capabilities.

An agent that has to do one of these needs an unscoped credential, which is a
choice its owner makes on purpose. A credential limited to named abilities also
sees only those in core's abilities list and in the MCP tool list.

A refusal is a 403 with the code `scope` (`tp_scope` on core routes; a tool
error over MCP) and says which grant is missing. Without `personal`, emails and
restricted fields are left out of every row, user and comment, and a filter,
sort or search on one is a 403 rather than a quiet probe.

Application passwords made before TypedPress's flows, and any created by other
clients or plugins outside TypedPress's flows, have no scope and work exactly as
WordPress ships them. A scoped password signs in only where its scope is
enforced: with the app plugin deactivated it is refused, never widened. The
refusal lives in the `typedpress-runtime` plugin, so removing that plugin (by
someone with file or WP-CLI access; a scoped credential can't) leaves a scoped
password an ordinary one. Revoke agent passwords before uninstalling TypedPress.

### Connect a client

The steps are the `typedpress-connect-mcp` skill, which `typedpress init` writes into the
project: `skills/typedpress-connect-mcp/SKILL.md`
finds the endpoint, creates a scoped agent credential and builds the header
without writing the password down, and
`references/clients.md`
has the configuration for Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Codex.

### Check an endpoint by hand

The endpoint is MCP over Streamable HTTP. `POST` an `initialize` request with
the `Authorization` header, `Content-Type: application/json` and
`Accept: application/json, text/event-stream`. Later requests repeat the
`Mcp-Session-Id` header the answer carried and send `MCP-Protocol-Version` with
the negotiated version. The repository's
`mcp-proof.mjs` does exactly
that against any built TypedPress app (`TP_SITE`, `TP_APP`, `TP_TOOL`, and
`TP_APP_PASSWORD=user:application-password` in the environment), and prints
the `initialize` answer, the tool names and one tool call:

```jsonl
{"endpoint":"http://localhost:8794/wp-json/mcp/typedpress-pantry"}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":0,"result":{"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","capabilities":{"prompts":{"listChanged":false},"resources":{"subscribe":false,"listChanged":false},"tools":{"listChanged":false}},"serverInfo":{"name":"Pantry","version":"0.3.0"},"instructions":"TypedPress app pantry"}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"tools":[{"name":"pantry-locations-list"},{"name":"pantry-locations-get"},{"name":"pantry-locations-create"},{"name":"pantry-locations-update"},{"name":"pantry-locations-delete"},{"name":"pantry-items-list"},{"name":"pantry-items-get"},{"name":"pantry-items-create"},{"name":"pantry-items-update"},{"name":"pantry-items-delete"},{"name":"pantry-shopping-list-list"},{"name":"pantry-shopping-list-get"},{"name":"pantry-shopping-list-create"},{"name":"pantry-shopping-list-update"},{"name":"pantry-shopping-list-delete"},{"name":"pantry-consume"},{"name":"pantry-expiring-soon"},{"name":"pantry-media-list"},{"name":"pantry-media-get"},{"name":"pantry-media-delete"}]}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"{\"rows\":[]}"}],"isError":false,"structuredContent":{"rows":[]}}}
```

`tests/wp/abilities.test.ts` runs the same exchange on every change.

## Read pages as Markdown

While a TypedPress app is active, every public URL WordPress renders also has a
Markdown version at the same address plus `.md`:

| HTML URL                 | Markdown URL               |
|--------------------------|----------------------------|
| `/hello-world/`          | `/hello-world.md`          |
| `/`                      | `/index.md`                |
| `/category/news/?page=2` | `/category/news.md?page=2` |

- **Single posts and pages** show the title, then the stored content. Blocks
  Markdown can write come out as Markdown. Any other block comes out as the
  text, links and images of its rendered HTML. Raw HTML never comes through.
- **Archives, the blog index and search results** list each entry with a link
  to its own `.md` URL, plus links to the previous and next pages.
- **Only public content gets a Markdown URL.** Drafts, previews, private posts,
  feeds and TypedPress collections get a 404. A password-protected post shows only
  its title, even to a visitor who entered the password.
- **The `.md` URL is its own URL, the same for every visitor.** It is rendered
  as a signed-out visitor, even for a signed-in request. Page caches store it
  apart from the HTML.

Each HTML page links its Markdown version, so agents can find it:

```text
Link: <https://your-site.example/hello-world.md>; rel="alternate"; type="text/markdown"
<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown" href="https://your-site.example/hello-world.md" />
```

On Spacefast, `Accept: text/markdown` on the HTML URL returns the same
Markdown. That response is never cached. Elsewhere, request the `.md` URL.

`/llms.txt` lists the site, then the newest 100 entries of each public post
type, and each public taxonomy's terms. Every entry links to its Markdown URL.

HTML pages, Markdown pages, `/llms.txt` and `robots.txt` send a
[Content-Signal](https://contentsignals.org/) of
`search=yes, ai-input=yes, ai-train=no`. To change it, filter
`tp_content_signal` in a plugin; return `''` to send none:

```php
add_filter('tp_content_signal', fn () => 'search=yes, ai-input=no, ai-train=no');
```

fields.title: Live updates
fields.description: Reads that stay current without a reload.

record.body:
A page can keep a read current while other people write. Subscribe to it, and the callback gets the result now and again each time it changes, always as the signed-in visitor reads it: ```ts import { createClient } from "./tp/_generated/client/index.ts"; const first = createClient(); const stop = first.todos.list({ where: { done: false }, orderBy: { createdAt: "asc" } }).subscribe( (todos) => render(todos), (error) => report(error), ); // later: stop(); ``` Every read is a `Query`: `await` it for one answer, or `subscribe(onData, onError?)` to keep it current. `list`, `paginate`, `get` and `count` all work the same way. A read is sent when it is first awaited or subscribed to, not when it is made, so to run two at once, await them together (`await Promise.all([first.posts.list(), first.authors.list()])`). ```ts first.todos.count({ where: { done: false } }).subscribe((open) => badge(open)); first.todos.get(42).subscribe((todo) => show(todo), (error) => error.status === 404 && gone()); ``` - A subscription refreshes after a write to its kind, to a kind it loads through `with`, or to a kind a relation filter in `where` looks into. - Every subscription of a client travels in one request, however many there are. Two subscriptions to the same read share one. - `onError` gets the problem of a read the server refuses, and network failures. The subscription continues. A `get` whose row is missing, or which the visitor may not read, is a 404. - A write made through the same client (`create`, `update`, `delete`, an action) refreshes the subscriptions that read that kind as soon as it returns. - A sign-in or sign-out refreshes every subscription, as the new visitor, also when another client on the same session storage made it. An answer to a request sent as the previous visitor is dropped. - A subscriber whose callback (`onData` or `onError`) throws doesn't stop the others: the error is reported as uncaught (`reportError`), and the subscription continues. - `paginate({ offset })` can be awaited but not subscribed to (`subscribe` throws): subscribe to a page by `cursor`. - `first.todos.watch(query, onRows, onError?)` is `first.todos.list(query).subscribe(onRows, onError)`. For a read that isn't a kind query, such as an action's result or a global, use the exported `watch` helper with the kinds the read depends on. It re-runs the read itself: ```ts import { createClient, watch } from "./tp/_generated/client/index.ts"; const first = createClient(); watch(first, ["todos"], () => first.actions.openCount(), (count) => badge(count)); ``` ## Optimistic updates Show a write before the server has answered, and take it back if it fails: ```ts const open = first.todos.list({ where: { done: false } }); const pending = open.optimistic((todos) => [...todos, { id: -1, title, done: false }]); try { await first.todos.create({ title }); pending.settle(); // kept until the server's next answer replaces it } catch (error) { pending.rollback(); // subscribers get the server's data back } ``` The update applies to what subscribers of that read are shown, and to the read's first answer when it hasn't arrived yet. It changes nothing on the server, and it does nothing when no one is subscribed to the read. ## How fresh | | Another visitor's write shows after | Your own write shows after | |----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------| | No transport (plain WordPress hosting) | 2 to 30 seconds | one request | | A transport, live | the notice's delivery plus one request | one request | | A hidden tab | when it is shown again | | Without a transport the client asks on an interval that adapts: 2 seconds after a change, half as long again after each answer that changed nothing, up to 30 seconds, each wait jittered by 20%. Errors double the wait. A hidden tab does not ask at all, and asks once when it is shown again. That includes a page opened in a background tab or prerendered: a subscription made there sends nothing until the page is shown (a seed is shown at once). A page restored from the back/forward cache asks again, since it may have been frozen for a long time. This is not a socket. On hosting without a push transport, another visitor's write never shows in under about two seconds, and a quiet page can be 30 seconds behind. If you need updates faster than that, your host has to supply a transport. ## React hooks, for a React frontend outside TypedPress TypedPress's own pages (`tp/app/`) never run React: they compile to PHP and the Interactivity API, and keep data live with `` and `useLive`. The hooks here are for a React app that runs somewhere else and uses TypedPress as its backend: Next.js, TanStack Start, an Astro island, Vite. `typedpress build` writes them to `tp/_generated/client/react.ts`. The file imports nothing from `"react"`. You hand it your React, so a project that never imports it needs no React, and the hooks use the React your app already bundles: ```tsx // first.ts import * as React from "react"; import { createClient } from "./tp/_generated/client/index.ts"; import { createHooks } from "./tp/_generated/client/react.ts"; export const first = createClient({ url: "https://example.com/__tp/api/v1" }); export const { useQuery, useMutation } = createHooks(React); ``` ```tsx function Todos() { const open = first.todos.list({ where: { done: false }, orderBy: { createdAt: "asc" } }); const todos = useQuery(open); const add = useMutation((title: string) => first.todos.create({ title }), { optimistic: (apply, title) => apply(open, (rows) => [...rows, { id: -1, title, done: false }]), }); if (todos.loading) return

Loading…

; if (todos.error) return

{todos.error.detail}

; return ( <>
    {todos.data?.map((todo) =>
  • {todo.title}
    • )}
); } ``` - **`useQuery(read, options?)`** subscribes to a read and returns `{ data, error, loading }`. Build the read inline: it is re-subscribed only when the call or its arguments change. `data` is kept while a later refresh fails on the network, and cleared when the server refuses the read (401, 403, 404), as after a sign-out. Pass `null`, or `{ enabled: false }`, to subscribe to nothing. `{ seed: { token, data } }` shows a server-rendered answer at once. - **`useMutation(write, options?)`** returns `{ mutate, pending, error, reset }`. `optimistic` runs before the write is sent; each `apply(read, update)` changes what subscribers of that read are shown. When the write succeeds the change stays until the server's answer replaces it. When it fails the change is taken back and `mutate` rejects with the error. - Every `useQuery` on a page shares one request to the server, and a render happens only when a result changed. - React 18 and later. The hooks use `useSyncExternalStore`, so they are safe under concurrent rendering and render the seed, or the loading state, on the server. Freshness is the client's: 2 to 30 seconds for another visitor's write without a push transport, one request for your own. ## Transports TypedPress ships no realtime transport. A host delivers change notices with one. While it is live, a notice refreshes the subscriptions that read the kinds it names at once, and the interval becomes a slow safety poll. ```ts import { createClient, registerRealtimeTransport, type RealtimeTransport } from "./tp/_generated/client/index.ts"; const transport: RealtimeTransport = { connect(deliver, status) { const socket = new WebSocket("wss://relay.example/tp"); socket.onopen = () => status("live"); socket.onclose = () => status("down"); socket.onmessage = (event) => deliver(JSON.parse(event.data)); return () => socket.close(); }, }; createClient({ realtime: { transport } }); // this client only registerRealtimeTransport(transport); // every client on the page, including ones created earlier ``` | Option | Default | Meaning | |-----------------------|---------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `realtime.pollMs` | adaptive, 2 to 30 s | `{ min, max }` sets the bounds in milliseconds, a number a fixed interval, `false` turns polling off | | `realtime.livePollMs` | 60000 | the safety poll while the transport is live, jittered ±20%; a notice lost in transit costs at most that delay; `false` turns it off | | `realtime.transport` | the registered one | `false` turns the transport off | A client connects its transport only while something is subscribed. When the transport goes from down to live, subscriptions refresh once to catch up. A notice only says which kinds to ask about: the data always comes from the visitor's own read. Spacefast's Cast transport does not register for TypedPress builds yet: its engine still runs the 0.3.0 compiler, and the names it uses are the 0.3.0 ones (host checklist, item 7). Until that changes, subscriptions on Spacefast poll like on any other host. ## Server side: the subscription endpoint Polling without a transport does not repeat each read. One request, `POST /__tp/api/v1/_live`, carries every read a page is subscribed to with the token of the answer it last got, and answers each with "not modified" or the fresh result, evaluated as the caller: ```http POST /__tp/api/v1/_live { "queries": [{ "kind": "todos", "op": "list", "args": { "where": { "done": false } }, "token": "…" }] } { "data": { "results": [{ "changed": false, "token": "…" }], "poll": { "minMs": 2000, "maxMs": 30000 } } } ``` `op` is `list`, `paginate`, `get` or `count`, with the arguments of that call on a kind. A result is `{ changed: true, token, data }`, `{ changed: false, token }`, `{ error }` (the read's problem document) or `{ pending: true }` (the request ran out of time; ask again). A request takes at most 20 queries. Tokens are opaque: keep the latest one per query and send it back. TypedPress keeps a change counter per kind, written in the same transaction as every write through its write path, including wp-admin and core REST saves of your kinds. A read whose kinds the caller may read in full is answered from the counters without running. Any other read (a kind with a field hidden from the caller, a rule that gives them only some rows) runs on each poll and is compared with what the caller last got, so an answer never says that something changed which the caller may not read. A write made outside TypedPress's write path, such as another plugin's SQL, is seen within five minutes. PHP code can ask the same question without HTTP, for example to render a read and hand its token to the browser: ```php $results = \TypedPress\Live\Module::evaluate($db, $viewer, [['kind' => 'todos', 'op' => 'list', 'args' => ['limit' => 20]]]); // [['changed' => true, 'token' => '…', 'data' => …, 'json' => '…']] ``` The design, its measured cost and what it is not are in the decision record. ## Server side: the change hook After a transaction commits, the runtime fires one WordPress action for the whole transaction: ```php add_action('tp_realtime_changes', static function (array $notice): void { // ['id' => '…', 'at' => '2026-11-07T10:00:00.000Z', 'changes' => [ // ['collection' => 'todos', 'ops' => ['create', 'update'], 'ids' => [12, 13]], // ]] }); ``` Every pipeline write reports: REST and action writes, hooks, jobs, the CLI and wp-admin saves. A rolled-back transaction reports nothing. `collection` is the schema key the client uses (`client.`). A collection's `ids` becomes `null` when one transaction changes more than 100 of its rows, or any of its ids is longer than 191 characters. A transaction touching more than 64 collections is announced as several notices. Notices never carry row values. WordPress comments on a kind with `comments` report as `wp:comments`, with `ids: null`, when the approved thread changes: a comment approved, saved approved, edited while approved, unapproved, spammed, trashed or deleted. A comment held for moderation, or spam that was never approved, reports nothing. `wp:comments` is not a collection key; `` regions that show a `` thread ask again on it. A host can register a transport in PHP instead of hooking the action: ```php \TypedPress\Realtime\Module::publish(new class implements \TypedPress\Realtime\Publisher { public function publish(array $notice): void { /* send it */ } }); ``` Publishers run after commit, on the request that wrote, so keep them fast and bounded. A publisher that throws is logged and never fails the write. With no publisher and no listener on the action, the runtime collects nothing. ### Shared rooms A host that sends one notice to every viewer of a site should call `\TypedPress\Realtime\Module::shared($notice)` first. It keeps ids only for collections any visitor can list: read rule `anyone` and no drafts. For other collections `ids` becomes `null`, so a viewer learns that the collection changed, not which rows. Clients refresh the same way in both cases.

A TypedPress app can render its own front end from `tp/app/`: React-style TSX that the compiler turns into PHP, rendered by WordPress on each request. It is one way, TSX to WordPress. It is optional: without `tp/app/`, WordPress renders the site with its theme, and nothing here loads. ## `tp/app/` ```text tp/app/ ├── layout.tsx # wraps every page: export const metadata, default component ├── page.tsx # / ├── not-found.tsx # the 404 for URLs no route serves, and for notFound() ├── error.tsx # a render error (logged; the page shows only this) ├── about/page.tsx # /about ├── colophon/page.md # /colophon: a WordPress Page an editor can change ├── (marketing)/pricing/page.tsx # /pricing: a group adds no segment ├── notes/page.tsx # /notes?page=2, with export const search ├── notes/[slug]/page.tsx # /notes/: params.slug ├── docs/[[...path]]/page.tsx # /docs, /docs/a/b: params.path is a string[] ├── account/layout.tsx # export const guard = "subscriber" ├── api/notes/route.ts # export async function GET(req) { … } └── _lib/ # never routed: colocated helpers ``` | Name | Meaning | |-------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `page.tsx` | A route. It may also export `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` handlers for its URL. | | `page.md` | A route whose content is a WordPress Page (see [Markdown pages](#markdown-pages)). | | `route.ts` | HTTP handlers only (`GET`, `POST`, …), for a URL with no page. | | `layout.tsx` | Wraps every page below it, outermost first. May export `guard`. | | `not-found.tsx` | At the root only. | | `error.tsx` | The nearest one above a page renders when the page throws. | | `[x]` / `[...x]` / `[[...x]]` | One segment / one or more / zero or more (last folder only). | | `(group)` / `_private` | No URL segment / never routed. | Two files that serve one URL, a folder that shadows WordPress (`wp-admin`, `wp-json`, `feed`, …), a misspelled export (`metdata`) and a layout that wraps no page are build errors at the file, with the fix. ## A page ```tsx // tp/app/notes/[slug]/page.tsx import { db } from "typedpress"; import { Content, notFound, type PageProps, type RouteRequest } from "typedpress/app"; export const metadata = ({ params }: PageProps<"notes/[slug]">) => ({ title: params.slug, canonical: `/notes/${params.slug}` }); export default async function Note({ params }: PageProps<"notes/[slug]">) { const note = await db.query.notes.findFirst({ where: { slug: params.slug } }); if (!note) notFound(); return (

{note.title}

{note.dek &&

{note.dek}

}
); } export async function POST(req: RouteRequest) { return { status: 303, headers: { location: `/notes/${req.params.slug}?sent=1` } }; } ``` - Components are ordinary (async) functions. `&&`, `?:`, `??`, `.map`, `.length` and string methods work as in React; the HTML matches what React renders, byte for byte, which the parity tests check. - **Reads run as the visitor.** The router binds every read a render makes to the person viewing the page, so drafts, rows they may not read and masked fields never reach the HTML. - `notFound()` renders `not-found.tsx` with a 404. `redirect(url, status?)` redirects (302 by default). - `metadata` is an object or a function of the page's props: `title`, `description`, `canonical`, `robots: { index, follow }`. A layout's `title: { default, template: "%s · Site" }` wraps its pages' titles. - `export const search = { page: integer().default(1), q: text().optional() }` types the query string. A value a field refuses (`?page=abc`) reads as absent. - `guard` on a layout: a role (`"subscriber"`, `"editor"`, …), `"authenticated"`, or `({ user }) => boolean`. A signed-out visitor goes to the login page; a signed-in one gets a 403. - `` is an `` that, once JavaScript runs, swaps only the router region (`@wordpress/interactivity-router`). `` prefetches on hover. - `` renders numbered links to the other pages of a listing as a `
`: each is this URL with only `page` (or `param`) changed, page 1 drops it, the current page is `aria-current` and not a link, and Previous and Next appear only where there is a page to go to. Twelve pages show as `1 … 4 5 6 7 8 … 12`. The links are ``s: plain links without JavaScript, router navigation with it. - `` renders a post body through `the_content`. `` places a literal as written and runs anything else through `wp_kses_post`. `typedpress build` writes `tp/_generated/routes.d.ts`. With it, `` is checked against the app's routes and `PageProps<"notes/[slug]">` types `params`. Point TypeScript at TypedPress's JSX types: ```json { "compilerOptions": { "jsx": "react-jsx", "jsxImportSource": "typedpress" } } ``` ## Forms `
` posts to an action imported from your server code, and works without JavaScript: ```tsx import { useFormState } from "typedpress/app"; import { subscribe } from "../server"; export default function Page() { const state = useFormState(subscribe); return ( {state.error ?

{state.error.message}

: null} {state.result ?

Subscribed {state.result.email}

: null}
); } ``` - The form posts form-encoded to the action's endpoint (`/__tp/api/v1/actions/`), with a hidden `_tp_return` (the page's path and query). The action runs as the visitor, exactly as a JSON call runs it, and the answer is `303 See Other` back to that page. - Fields read as the action's input types them: `integer()` and `number()` from their digits, `boolean()` from a checkbox (unchecked is `false`), select and reference lists from repeated names, an empty field as absent. A value that doesn't parse reaches the action's validation, which names the field. Uploads are refused (415); use the media API. - What came back is a flash: a cookie sealed with the site's key, named by `?_flash=` on the redirect, read once and deleted, gone after two minutes. Nothing is stored on the server. The marked URL is never served from or stored in a shared cache. - `useFormState(action)` reads it: `{ pending, error, result, values }`. `error.fields` maps the field an input error is about to its message; `values` refills the form and never holds a password field. `pending` is `false` on the server; the JavaScript submit sets it. - A page with a form stays cacheable for signed-out visitors: it carries no nonce. A page rendered for a signed-in user carries the REST nonce; without it, the action runs signed out. A post with another site's `Origin` is refused. - A `"use client"` component calls its action from `onSubmit` instead; `method` and `encType` on a form with an action are build errors. ## Comments ```tsx import { Comments, type PageProps } from "typedpress/app"; export default function Note({ item }: PageProps<"notes/[slug]">) { return

{item.title}

; } ``` `` renders the item's thread as the visitor may read it (approved comments, plus their own held ones) and a form that works without JavaScript. The item's kind must turn `comments` on; otherwise the build stops at the prop. Who may comment, moderation and reply depth belong to the kind, not the component, and are enforced wherever a comment is created: the form, the API and core's comment form all give the same answer. `comments: true` is signed-in users only, first-time moderation, and replies three levels deep (a deeper reply is refused); `comments: { guests, moderation, threaded, closeAfterDays }` changes any of them (Comments). See the decision. ## Search ```tsx import { integer, text } from "typedpress"; import { Search, SearchResults, type PageProps } from "typedpress/app"; export const search = { q: text().optional(), page: integer().default(1) }; export default function Find({ search }: PageProps) { return
; } ``` `` is a search form that works without JavaScript: a `GET` of this page (or `action`, a path on this site) with the query in `q`, never WordPress's own `s`. The input takes at most 200 characters. `` lists the rows that match, as the visitor may read them: - a draft, or a match only in a field the visitor may not read, never shows and isn't counted; - each result is its title, linked to its kind's URL, so `kind` must be a kind with a `url` (the build says so at the prop otherwise; for anything else, render the rows yourself with `kind.list({ search })`); - one kind pages with `page`, the same parameter as ``, and its links keep `q`; - with no `kind`, every searchable kind with a URL: up to `perPage` (10) rows each, under the kind's name, with a link to the rest at `?q=…&kind=`. A `kind=` the search doesn't cover finds nothing; - an empty `q` (or only spaces) renders nothing and reads nothing; a `q` longer than 200 characters, typed into the URL, shows a short message. Matching is by word prefix (`gard` finds "gardens"), and the first 8 words of a query count. On MySQL and MariaDB, words shorter than the server's minimum (3 characters on InnoDB) and its stopwords don't match. A page that searched (a non-empty `q`) is the visitor's alone: `private, no-store`, `noindex` (header and meta tag), and never recorded for page-cache purges, since every distinct query would be one more cached URL listing the kind. The bare form page is cached like any other. See the decision. ## Live regions ```tsx import { notes } from "typedpress:db"; import { Live } from "typedpress/app"; export default async function Home() { const all = await notes.list({ orderBy: { id: "asc" } }); return
    {all.map((n) =>
  • {n.title}
    • )}
; } ``` `` marks part of a server page the browser keeps current. When something the page read for it changes, the region is rendered again on the server, as the visitor, and the page updates in place through the Interactivity router. Client components and form fields in the page keep their state. `id` is a literal (lowercase letters, digits, dashes) and unique on the page. - **When it updates.** Each region subscribes with the kinds its page read. With a realtime transport it updates on the next change notice for one of them, or after a write the visitor makes through the typed client. Without one it updates on the next poll, 2 to 30 seconds apart. `` inside a region updates when a comment's approval changes. A region whose page read nothing updates on the poll only. Anything that changes without a TypedPress write (the clock, another plugin's SQL) shows within five minutes. - **What it costs.** A page with a live region makes one uncached request to WordPress when it loads, then one per poll while the tab is visible (or on a notice), per open tab. That holds even when the page itself came from a page cache, and that first request is what brings a cached copy current. A tab opened in the background, or prerendered, costs nothing until it is shown; a page restored with the browser's back button asks once. An unchanged region usually costs no render (the change counters answer). A region that reads something the counters can't follow, such as a comment thread, renders once per poll. Think about this before putting `` on a busy cached page. - At most four regions render per request; a page with more fills the rest on the next request. See the decision. ## Markdown pages ```md --- title: Colophon description: How this site is made. --- Set in a system font, served by **WordPress**. ``` A `page.md` is a real WordPress Page. The file is its first version: the first request after a build stores the Markdown as blocks in a Page, with the front matter as its title, excerpt and status. From then on an editor changes it in wp-admin, in the block editor, and the route shows what they saved. - It renders inside the `layout.tsx` files above it, and a layout's `guard` protects it, like a `page.tsx`. Its `` and description come from the stored Page, so an editor's change to either shows. - Front matter: `title`, `description`, `status` (`published` or `draft`), `canonical`, `robots: { index, follow }` and `id` (keeps the Page when the file moves to another URL). Without `title`, the first `# Heading` is the title. Any other key is a build error at its line: fields of your own belong to a kind with `sync`, where they have a type. - A later version of the file replaces the Page only while nobody edited the Page on the site. An edited Page keeps the site's version, and the log names the file. Removing the file leaves the Page in WordPress; nothing is deleted. The exception is taking a page away from visitors: a file that newly says `status: draft`, or moves under a `guard`, unpublishes an edited Page too, and leaves its text alone. - The route's path is the Page's address. WordPress's own address for it redirects there, and the editor's Preview button shows unsaved changes on the route. - A draft is a 404 for visitors and shows to people who can edit it. A Page under a `guard` is stored private, so WordPress's REST API, search, sitemap and feeds never list it. A password set in wp-admin locks the body for every visitor. - It has a Markdown twin at `/colophon.md` and a line in `/llms.txt` when anyone may read it, and none otherwise. - A `page.md` is one page with one URL, so it can't sit below `[slug]`. For many Markdown files, sync a folder into a kind and render it from a `page.tsx`. The ruling and its alternatives are in the decision. ## Stylesheets and images ```tsx // tp/app/layout.tsx import "./site.css"; // tp/app/notes/[slug]/page.tsx import styles from "./note.module.css"; import compass from "./compass.svg"; <article className={styles.note}><img src={compass} alt="" /></article> ``` - `import "./x.css"` links the stylesheet on every page whose page or layouts import it, directly or through a component. Each file is linked once, in import order, the root layout's first. - `import styles from "./x.module.css"` renames each class to `<file stem>_<class>` (`note.module.css`'s `.dek` is `note_dek`), and `styles.dek` is that name. If two modules define the same class name, the later one by path gets a number (`note_dek2`). A `"use client"` component may import a CSS module, and its class can depend on state. - `import logo from "./x.svg"` gives the file's URL. - Every file is copied into the app plugin under `tp/app/assets/`, named by a hash of its bytes, with a year's cache. A changed file gets a new URL. - These are refused at the line, with the fix: `@import` (import each file from TSX), a relative `url(...)` (put the file in `public/` and write `url(/name.png)`), `:global`, `:local` and `composes` in a module, and an SVG imported by a `"use client"` component (pass the URL as a prop).
