Other files, binary images and fonts among them, go in `public/`, by their URL. ## On WordPress The router answers on `template_redirect`, before the theme. wp-admin, login, `/wp-json`, feeds, robots and TypedPress's own paths never reach it. When `tp/app/` exists, a URL no route serves renders `not-found.tsx`. URLs WordPress itself resolves (a post, a category archive) keep the theme until a route serves them. The site's sitemap is WordPress's own, `/wp-sitemap.xml`. It lists the app's pages that have no parameters and no `guard` and render for a signed-out visitor, unless the page's metadata says `robots: { index: false }`, and the items of every kind with a `url` that a signed-out visitor may read. A draft, a row an access rule hides and a password-protected item are never in it. ### WordPress identity Each `page.tsx` route without parameters is also a **hidden, code-owned WordPress Page**, so the rest of WordPress sees the page as one of its own. - Menus, SEO plugins and `get_permalink()` see a normal published Page whose link and canonical URL are the route's URL. `/` is the front page (`page_on_front`), unless the site already chose a front page of its own. - The Page keeps its ID across builds, so a menu item that points at it keeps working. Its title is the page's literal `metadata.title`, else its folder name. - The route ID is the folder path (`notes/featured`). A page that sets its own keeps its Page when the file moves: `export const route = { id: "notes.featured" }` in a `page.tsx`, or `id: notes.featured` in a `page.md`'s front matter. The old URL then redirects to the new one. Two pages with one ID are a build error at the second. - A route under a layout `guard` stores its Page private, so search, feeds, the REST API and the sitemap never list it. - Code Pages are absent from the wp-admin Pages list, its counts and REST `context=edit` lists. `edit_post` and `delete_post` are denied on them, and a write that bypasses capabilities keeps the stored fields. - WordPress's own addresses for the Page (its slug, `?page_id=`) redirect to the route. - A route that goes away moves its Page to the trash; nothing is deleted. A URL that another published Page already owns is not taken over: the route still renders, without a Page, and the log says so. A `page.md` route owns a real Page that editors change ([Markdown pages](#markdown-pages)); a route with parameters has no Page. ## Client components A file that starts with `"use client"` is a client component. Its first render is ordinary server HTML; in the browser the WordPress Interactivity API takes it over in place, with no second render and no bundle of its own. ```tsx // tp/components/CheerButton.tsx "use client"; import { useState } from "typedpress/client"; import { cheer } from "../actions"; export function CheerButton({ noteId, count: initial }: { noteId: number; count: number }) { const [count, setCount] = useState(initial); const [busy, setBusy] = useState(false); return ( <button type="button" disabled={busy} onClick={async () => { setBusy(true); setCount((await cheer({ noteId })).count); setBusy(false); }}> {count === 1 ? "1 cheer" : `${count} cheers`} </button> ); } ``` - `useState`, values derived from state and props, handlers, `useEffect`, `useMount`, `useEvent`, `useRef` and `sharedState` come from `"typedpress/client"`. - `useLive(kind, query, { enabled })` is a list read the page keeps current, as `{ data, error, loading }`. The server answers it in the first render as the visitor (`TypedPress\Live\Module::evaluate`, with its token), and the page subscribes to the same read through the app's typed client (`@typedpress/client`), so another visitor's write shows with no reload: within the client's poll (2 to 30 seconds) without a push transport, at once with one. The query reads props and literals, which both sides have; a query that follows state is a build error for now. There is no `seed` option: the server's answer is the seed. The names match the generated client's React `useQuery`, for external React frontends. - Calling an imported action posts to its endpoint with the REST nonce, as the visitor. - A list over state or props, `items.map((item) => <li key={item.id}>…</li>)`, and a conditional over elements, `{open && <p>…</p>}` or `{empty ? <em>…</em> : <b>…</b>}`, re-render in the browser from a `<template>`. Each item and each branch is one element; each item has a `key`. - The component returns one element. React context, third-party React components, npm imports and `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` are refused at the line. See rendering.md §4.1 for the full mapping and `examples/full-site` for a site that uses one. ## Static output Pages render on WordPress per request by default. Two settings prebuild them instead, in [Astro](https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/on-demand-rendering/)'s words. The design and measurements are in the decision record. | You want | Write | |----------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------| | Some pages prebuilt, the rest rendered per request, on one WordPress | `export const prerender = true` in those pages | | A whole site as static files, with no WordPress serving it | `defineConfig({ output: "static" })`, then `typedpress export` | | Static files from a WordPress that editors use somewhere else | the same, with `typedpress export --site https://cms.example.com` | A prebuilt page is what a signed-out visitor sees, rendered by the page's own compiled code. So it can't depend on the request. These are build errors at the page, each with its fix: - a layout `guard` above the page; - `export const search`; - a dynamic segment the build can't list; - calling `is_user_logged_in`, `current_user_can` or `get_current_user_id`. ### Which URLs a dynamic page has A page whose folders serve a kind's `url` (`notes/[slug]` for `url: "/notes/:slug"`) is built once per item a signed-out visitor may read. Drafts and rows an access rule hides are never built. Any other dynamic page lists its URLs with `staticParams`, Astro's `getStaticPaths`: ```tsx // tp/app/tags/[tag]/page.tsx import type { PageProps, StaticParams } from "typedpress/app"; export const prerender = true; export async function staticParams(): Promise<StaticParams<"tags/[tag]">> { return ["field", "lab notes"].map((tag) => ({ tag })); } export default function Tag({ params }: PageProps<"tags/[tag]">) { return <h1>{params.tag}</h1>; } ``` `staticParams` runs as a signed-out visitor, so it can read the database. ### Prebuilt pages on WordPress (`prerender = true`) - **When the files are made.** After a deploy, an Action Scheduler action renders each prebuilt URL and writes its HTML and Markdown to `wp-content/cache/typedpress-prebuilt/`. - **How they are served.** The app answers from the file before WordPress parses the request, with the same `Cache-Control` as a cacheable render and the header `X-TypedPress-Prebuilt: 1`. - **What still renders per request.** A signed-in visitor, a request with a query string, and a URL whose file isn't written yet. - **After a write.** A write that changes what a prebuilt page shows deletes that page's files at once and schedules its rebuild. Until the rebuild runs, the page renders per request, so nobody sees the old content. Other pages keep their files. - **The rest of the site.** Markdown twins, `llms.txt` and the sitemap are unchanged. - **Hosts that can't reach their own address.** The rebuild fetches the page from the site's own address. A host where that fails sets the `tp_prebuild_url` filter. ### A static site (`typedpress export`) ```sh typedpress export # writes tp/dist/static/ typedpress export --site-url https://docs.example.com # also writes sitemap.xml and canonical links typedpress export --base /docs # for a site served below /docs/ ``` The project must say `output: "static"`, where every page is prebuilt. `prerender = false` is a build error there. - **Where the content comes from.** Without `--site`, `typedpress export` starts a throwaway WordPress on SQLite (the one `typedpress dev` uses) with the build installed and `tp/content/` loaded, renders every page, and removes the site. - **The URL layout.** It is the one GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages and most static servers answer. | URL | File | |-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `/` | `index.html`, with `index.md` | | `/docs/intro` | `docs/intro.html`, with `docs/intro.md` | | an unknown URL | `404.html` | | `/llms.txt`, `/robots.txt`, `/sitemap.xml` | the files of those names; `sitemap.xml` only with `--site-url` | | a moved item's old URL | a line in `_redirects`, and a page that redirects in the browser | | stylesheets, images, fonts, the Interactivity API and router modules, client component stores | the path WordPress serves them from (`wp-content/…`, `wp-includes/…`) | **What a static page can't do.** The export refuses each of these with the page and the fix: - **A client component that calls an action.** There is no server. With `--site`, a public action (`access: "anyone"`) is called on the hosted site instead. - **A link to a URL the export doesn't contain.** For example a page left out, or WordPress's sign-in or comment form. With `--site`, sign-in, comment and `wp-admin` links go to the hosted site. - **A page that redirects, or that `staticParams` lists but that renders a 404.** ### WordPress as the CMS (`typedpress export --site`) Editors work on a hosted WordPress running the app. `typedpress export --site https://cms.example.com` renders that site's published content with this checkout's pages. - **Credentials.** It signs in as an editor the way `typedpress sync` does: the credential `typedpress login` stored, or `TP_APP_PASSWORD` (`user:application-password`) or `TP_TOKEN` in CI. - **The site must run this checkout's build.** Otherwise the export stops and says to deploy first. - **Rebuilding on publish.** Add the hosted site's `webhooks` config to call a CI job on publish (`events: ["*"]`). The job runs `typedpress export --site …` and uploads `tp/dist/static/`. - **Client components** call public actions on the hosted site, across origins. - **Comments and sign-in** happen on the hosted site. - **Guarded pages** can't be exported: a static file is the same for everyone. ## Publish on Spacefast `tp/app/` is ordinary app source. `typedpress sources` captures the pages, components, stylesheets and SVGs with the rest of the app, and the host's `typedpress compile-sources` compiles them into the app plugin, with no Node and no separate render step. The compiled manifest lists every page in `pagePaths` and every handler in `routes`, so the host can hand those URLs to WordPress. ## From the old `pages/` renderer The separate `pages/` renderer (`@typedpress/pages`, `typedpress-pages build` and `tp/pages.json`) is gone. A project that still has `pages/` beside `typedpress.config.ts` fails to build with the move as the fix, and a host refuses a capture that carries old-renderer pages. To port: | Before | Now | |--------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `pages/<path>/page.tsx` | `tp/app/<path>/page.tsx` | | `load({ content })` returning queries | `await db.query.<kind>…` in the page; reads run as the visitor | | `collectionPage("notes")` | `url: "/notes/:slug"` on the kind and `tp/app/notes/[slug]/page.tsx`, which receives `item` | | `<Show when={x}>`, `orElse(x, d)`, `count(list)` | `{x && …}`, `x ?? d`, `list.length` | | `<RichText value>` | `<Content value>` from `"typedpress/app"` | | `<Island>` with a hand-written store | a `"use client"` component | | `link("/x")` | `<Link href="/x">` from `"typedpress/app"` | | `generateMetadata` | `export const metadata = (props) => ({ … })` |

fields.title: Staged versions
fields.description: Prepare a change to an item and publish it later.

record.body:
A staged version is a change to an item that is saved beside the live item. Visitors, the API,
core REST, Markdown twins, feeds, search and caches keep returning the live item until someone
promotes the staged version. Until then it can be read, compared with the live item, previewed
through a signed link, scheduled, or discarded.

Every `collection()` has staged versions. `table()` kinds do not: a table row has no editorial
lifecycle, so a change to it is an update. Turn the feature off for one collection with
`staged: false`.

```ts
export const posts = collection({ title: text(), body: richText() }, { url: "/blog/:slug" });
export const logs = collection({ title: text() }, { staged: false });
```

## What a staged version is

- **One per item, shared.** Everyone who may update the item reads and writes the same staged
  version. Each `stage` call adds its fields to it; a field staged again takes the new value.
- **Only the staged fields.** The staged version holds the fields that were staged. Promoting it
  changes those fields and no others, so a live edit to another field made in the meantime stays.
- **A WordPress revision.** It is stored as one revision of the post, named
  `<id>-autosave-staged-v1`, with its own internal status `typedpress-staged` where core's revisions
  have `inherit`. Core reads revisions by that status, so its revision lists and count, the
  `/autosaves` route the block editor takes the user's autosave from, wp-admin's revision screen
  and its Restore, revision pruning, change detection and wp-admin's revision upgrade all pass
  over it. It is separate from core's own per-user autosave slot, which the editors overwrite and
  delete. A promote or discard gives it core's status and an ordinary revision's name. Staged
  revisions saved before the status existed get it when the runtime updates. Its fields are stored on the revision
  under the same meta keys the post uses, as on every other revision of a TypedPress post.
  `_tp_staged` on the revision records the staged fields and a scheduled promote.

## Operations

All of these need the item's `update` rule. A caller it doesn't cover gets the `404` a missing item
gets, whether or not anything is staged.

| Operation                 | API (`/__tp/api/v1`)                                                   | Client                             | Ability `<app>/<kind>-…` | `wp typedpress staged …`                          |
|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------|----------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| Stage                     | `PATCH /<kind>/<id>/staged` with the fields                            | `client.posts.stage(id, patch)`    | `stage`                    | `stage <kind> <id> <json>`                          |
| Read                      | `GET /<kind>/<id>/staged`                                              | `client.posts.staged(id)`          | `staged-get`               | `show <kind> <id>`                                  |
| Compare                   | `GET /<kind>/<id>/staged/compare`                                      | `client.posts.compare(id)`         | `staged-compare`           | `compare <kind> <id>`                               |
| Promote                   | `POST /<kind>/<id>/staged/promote`                                     | `client.posts.promote(id)`         | `staged-promote`           | `promote <kind> <id>`                               |
| Schedule a promote        | the same route with `{ "at": "<ISO time>" }`; `{ "at": null }` cancels | `client.posts.promote(id, { at })` | `staged-promote` with `at` | `promote <kind> <id> --at=<ISO time>` or `--cancel` |
| Discard                   | `DELETE /<kind>/<id>/staged`                                           | `client.posts.discard(id)`         | `staged-discard`           | `discard <kind> <id>`                               |
| Preview link              | `POST /<kind>/<id>/staged/preview` with optional `{ "ttl": seconds }`  | `client.posts.previewLink(id)`     | `staged-preview`           |                                                     |
| List every staged version |                                                                        |                                    |                            | `list [<kind>]`                                     |

`wp typedpress staged` is the trusted CLI: it applies no access rule and no field mask.

A staged version reads as:

```json
{
  "id": 412,
  "row": { "id": 7, "title": "Staged title", "slug": "hello", "status": "published" },
  "fields": ["title"],
  "by": { "id": 3, "name": "Ed" },
  "at": "2026-11-13T10:00:00.000Z",
  "promoteAt": null
}
```

`row` is the item as it would be once promoted. `id` is the revision that holds it.

### Stage

`stage` checks the patch as an update would: the update rule given the patch, field write rules,
types, `min`/`max`/`pattern`/`validate`, media and references. It runs no hook, queues no webhook
and purges no URL, because nothing visible changed. `status`, `publishedAt` and the other system
fields can't be staged: they change with an update of the item.

Unique checks run when the staged version is promoted, not when it is staged: until then the value
is not in use.

### Compare

```json
{ "id": 412, "changes": [{ "field": "title", "live": "Live title", "staged": "Staged title" }], "by": {}, "at": "…", "promoteAt": null }
```

`changes` lists the staged fields whose value differs from the live item, in schema order. Both
sides go through the reader's field masks. A field hidden from the reader on either side is left
out, whether it changed or not.

### Promote

A promote is an update of the item by the caller, with the staged fields as the patch. So the
update rule, field write rules, validation, `beforeUpdate` and `afterUpdate`, unique checks, the
revision, URL purges, change notices, webhooks and core's `rest_insert_{type}` and
`rest_after_insert_{type}` hooks all run exactly as for `PATCH /<kind>/<id>`. The
update and the end of the staged version are one transaction: a promote that is refused changes
nothing and keeps the staged version.

The promoter needs to be allowed to write every staged field. An editor can't promote a staged
version that holds a field only admins may set.

After a promote the staged revision stays in the item's revisions, next to the revision the update
wrote.

### Schedule a promote

`{ "at": "2026-12-01T09:00:00Z" }` schedules the promote on WordPress's own `publish_future_post`
cron event, the one core uses for scheduled posts. No other cron, worker or queue is involved. The
caller must be able to promote now.

When the event runs, the promote runs as whoever scheduled it, under the rules as they are then:
the same user, a signed-out caller as a signed-out caller, and only the trusted CLI's own schedule
with the CLI's authority. A schedule that names nobody is refused. If it is refused or fails, nothing changes, the schedule is cleared, and the reason is kept
on the staged version as `error` for its editors. It is not retried. Staging more fields keeps the
schedule.

### Discard

`discard` ends the staged version. The live item is untouched. The revision stays in the item's
revisions and is recorded as discarded and by whom; nothing is deleted.

### Preview links

```json
{ "token": "…", "expiresAt": "…", "api": "https://example.com/__tp/api/v1/posts/7/staged?preview=…", "url": "https://example.com/blog/hello/?tp_preview=…" }
```

- `api` returns the staged version without signing in, through an anonymous visitor's field masks
  and without `by`, `promoteAt` or `error`. Use it from an external frontend or a `tp/app` page.
- `url` is the item's own page rendering the staged title, content and fields an anonymous visitor
  may read; a field hidden from them is blank there, staged or live. It is set for a
  kind with a `url` that the theme renders, and `null` otherwise.

A token is an HMAC over the kind, the item, the staged revision and an expiry, keyed with the
site's `AUTH` salt. It expires after an hour by default (`ttl`, 60 seconds to one day), and stops
working when the staged version is promoted or discarded, or when the site's salts change. A
previewed page is sent `no-store`, `noindex` and `no-referrer`, and is never stored by Batcache.
Markdown twins ignore the token.

## Read before you write: `_rev`

Every row of a collection the API, the client or an ability returns carries `_rev`, an opaque token
of the row as it was read. Send it back with a write to refuse the write if the row changed since:

| Write                                                                       | Where `_rev` goes                      | Which token                                               |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| `PATCH /<kind>/<id>`, `<kind>-update`                                       | in the body / input, beside the fields | the row's                                                 |
| `DELETE /<kind>/<id>`, `<kind>-delete`                                      | `?_rev=` / input                       | the row's                                                 |
| stage, promote, discard (API, abilities, `wp typedpress staged … --rev=`) | body, query or input                   | the staged version's (`_rev` of a stage, read or compare) |
| `POST /<kind>/<id>/revisions/<rid>/restore`                                 | body                                   | the row's                                                 |

A stale token is refused with `409 stale_revision`. The problem carries the row's current `_rev`
and `changed`: `fields`, the fields that differ since your read as you may read them (a field
hidden from you is never named, changed or not), and for a staged token `staged: true` when someone
else changed the staged version. Read again, look at what changed, and decide whether to retry.

With nothing staged, the row's own `_rev` is accepted where a staged one is expected, so a read
starts a stage. The row's `_rev` is the same for every reader and does not change when someone
stages, so it says nothing about whether a staged version exists.

Leaving `_rev` out is an unconditional write, as on WordPress's own routes.

## Edit locks

TypedPress uses WordPress's own edit lock, `_edit_lock`, which the block editor and the classic editor
set while someone has the item open and refresh with their heartbeat (it lapses 150 seconds after
the last one). While another user holds it, these are refused with `409 locked` and the holder
(`holder: { id, name }`):

- the API's update, delete, revision restore, stage, promote, discard and scheduled promote;
- the abilities for the same steps;
- core REST's update, delete and revision restore of the item (`/wp/v2/<post type>/<id>`).

Reading again does not clear it. Send `takeover: true` (`?takeover=1` on a DELETE, `takeover` in an
ability's input) to take the lock first, as the editor's **Take over** button does; the old holder's
editor then shows that someone took over. Both checks apply only to a caller the row's update rule
covers: anyone else gets the missing row's 404 and learns of no lock or token. The trusted CLI and
cron never meet a lock. wp-admin's own edit screen keeps WordPress's lock dialog.

## Who can tell that a staged version exists

Only a caller who passes the item's update rule, or who holds a valid preview token.

For anyone else nothing differs between an item with a staged version and one without: the item's
row, lists, counts, search, `?format=md`, the Markdown twin, the page, feeds, `llms.txt`, the
sitemap, core REST (including the item's `version-history` and `predecessor-version` links, which
core counts for every reader), and the `404` of every staged route and ability, also when the item's
update rule throws on the staged data.

Nor can they tell afterwards: a discarded or promoted staged revision stays in the item's history
for its editors, but core's links leave it out, so a discard leaves them as they were and a promote
moves them as one update does.

## Abilities and credentials

Each step is its own Ability, so a credential can be allowed to stage and not to promote:
`<app>/<kind>-stage`, `-staged-get`, `-staged-compare`, `-staged-promote`, `-staged-discard` and
`-staged-preview`. TypedPress declares them separately and does not scope credentials itself.

They are offered only to a caller whose update rule on the kind covers at least one row (or needs
the write's data to answer): core's abilities list, one ability's description and the MCP tools
list leave them out for anyone else, so a read-only caller never sees them.

## Limits

- Post kinds only. `table()` kinds and globals have no staged versions.
- Relations loaded with `with` are not part of a staged version; stage the referencing field.
- A staged version belongs to one row. On a kind with `locales`, that is one translation.

fields.title: Uploads
fields.description: Where uploaded files are stored and how they are served.

record.body:
`uploads` selects one durable backend for the app's private files and standard
WordPress media. Configure it on the server in `defineConfig`; browser clients
keep using `client.files.<resource>` and `client.media`. `file()` and `media()`
references work in both collections and SQL tables, with the same access rules.
The logical file resource and physical provider bucket are different concepts.

```ts
import { defineConfig, env } from "typedpress";

export default defineConfig({
  name: "catalog",
  uploads: {
    backend: "s3",
    bucket: env("UPLOAD_BUCKET"),
    region: "us-east-1",
    // For Garage, R2, MinIO and other compatible services:
    // endpoint: env("UPLOAD_ENDPOINT"), pathStyle: true,
    prefix: "catalog",
    credentials: {
      accessKeyId: env("UPLOAD_ACCESS_KEY_ID"),
      secretAccessKey: env("UPLOAD_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"),
      // sessionToken: env("UPLOAD_SESSION_TOKEN"),
    },
  },
});
```

Bucket, endpoint, region and prefix accept strings or `env()` references;
credentials require `env()`. Provision the bucket separately, keep public access
blocked, and grant the runtime GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject and
ListBucket within its prefix. TLS verification remains enabled. Set credentials
in each replica's process environment or WordPress configuration constants.
Their values never enter generated clients, schema descriptions or provider
error messages. All replicas must share the database and provider configuration.

The transport uses MIT-licensed AsyncAWS S3 3.5.0, scoped as `TypedPress\Vendor` and
pinned with its dependencies in the runtime Composer lock. `scripts/vendor.sh runtime` reproduces the committed bundle and licenses. No signer is implemented
in TypedPress. S3 reads/uploads stream with bounded memory and finite HTTP deadlines;
image processing still needs PHP's normal memory and temporary disk budget.

## Installation, activation and readiness

The provider adapter ships inside `typedpress-runtime`; no offload plugin, Composer run
or credentials are needed at build time. As with [plugin dependencies](/docs/reference/wordpress-plugins),
installing the generated artifact does not activate it. Deploy and activate the
manifest's dependencies, runtime and app in dependency order. Runtime registration
installs the site's namespace once and schedules one recurring cleanup action;
repeated requests/activation preserve that namespace, unrelated plugin options and
existing media. The adapter does not configure or activate another offload plugin.
Do not run competing upload-directory or attachment-offload integrations together.

Activation is not provider readiness. The deployment owner still provisions the
bucket and least-privilege grant, injects environment values on every replica,
and runs Action Scheduler reliably. TypedPress does not create cloud accounts, buckets,
IAM policies or migrate existing disk uploads. Before routing traffic, upload and
read a private file and image, generate a size on another replica, then delete
them. A successful build, plugin activation or schema response alone proves none
of those provider permissions. Configured S3 errors fail closed at the operation.

The disposable WordPress acceptance lane performs actual
provider setup: it initializes a pinned Garage node, creates its isolated bucket,
imports a dedicated test key and grants access. It repeats setup after objects
exist, then proves read/write/list/delete and image processing across replicas.
This is test provisioning, not a production cloud provisioning command.

## Dependency choice

The reviewed alternatives are existing PHP implementations; no JavaScript S3 or
WordPress offload implementation is translated or copied. The adapter calls
AsyncAWS's `S3Client::putObject`, `getObject`, `deleteObject` and `listObjectsV2`;
the SDK owns signing, HTTP and XML. It leaves file identity, grants, transactions
and durable cleanup with TypedPress's existing database owners. The exact SDK source is
[`43b1f00d16f2c5c05b37337ccdc2aa1b1a24a18a`](https://github.com/async-aws/s3/tree/43b1f00d16f2c5c05b37337ccdc2aa1b1a24a18a),
version 3.5.0 (MIT); Composer locks its transitives and scoped vendoring retains
licenses. See dependency reproduction.

Two maintained WordPress alternatives were inspected at fixed releases:

- [Human Made S3 Uploads 3.0.13](https://github.com/humanmade/S3-Uploads/tree/c09bd3057747b181eeb9c22e380da9d904ba260a)
  (GPL-2.0-or-later) provides an S3 stream wrapper, remote image editors and an
  existing-media migration CLI. `S3_UPLOADS_OBJECT_ACL` and
  `s3_uploads_is_attachment_private` support private objects;
  `s3_uploads_s3_client_params` can configure a compatible endpoint. Its
  `Plugin::add_s3_signed_params_to_attachment_url` issues expiring provider URLs
  (six hours by default), while `delete_attachment_files` and
  `Stream_Wrapper::unlink` delete objects during core's deletion hook. Stream
  flush writes to the pathname's object key. TypedPress would need to replace those
  URL, mutation and deletion lifecycles to preserve stable editor URLs, immutable
  rollback and after-commit deletion. Its attachment hooks also do not represent
  TypedPress's private file rows or their owner grants.
- [WP Offload Media Lite 3.4.4](https://plugins.svn.wordpress.org/amazon-s3-and-cloudfront/tags/3.4.4/)
  (GPLv2) has attachment upload/download/remove handlers, supports local-file
  removal, and can mark each variant private through
  `as3cf_upload_object_key_as_private`. `AS3CF_SETTINGS` can supply runtime
  settings; `as3cf_aws_s3_client_args` can customize the SDK. Its item/offloaded-file
  tables own provider manifests separately from TypedPress. In
  `classes/integrations/media-library.php`, `delete_attachment` invokes the
  remove-provider handler and deletes the item immediately. Adapting it requires
  an additional item source for private file rows and coordination of both
  manifests, grants and transaction lifecycles. The inspected release archive's
  SHA-256 is `8f7dd3b3929e51542f2148f2350eed400a0d8daa30d575d37db86da7f8296930`.

Both are useful attachment-offload products. Neither is adopted as a second
owner of TypedPress's upload state in this unit. The smaller SDK transport is the chosen
reuse boundary. These are source/API assessments, not claims that the alternative
plugins passed this project's replica acceptance test. No plugin settings or
existing provider media are overwritten to make the chosen adapter work.

## Serving and processing

Private files retain their existing MIME/size limits, uploader ownership and
five-minute signed API grants. S3 objects have opaque keys under a random site
namespace and hashed app identity. File rows remain in `tp__files`; attachment
manifests remain in WordPress postmeta. Metadata never depends on a replica's disk.

Media remains publicly readable, matching the existing media API. Its originals,
WordPress intermediate sizes, TypedPress focal crops, scaled originals and image-edit
backups live in the same backend. Stable API URLs serve those bytes through PHP,
with safe MIME/disposition headers. They can be saved in Gutenberg content without
expiring. They are not public S3 URLs. WordPress responsive-image URLs use the same
manifest, and a deleted/replaced variant stops resolving through the API.

Each request uses a private random directory under the system temporary directory
for upload validation and image processing. The standard WordPress upload,
sideload and attachment metadata hooks offload originals and derivatives before
successful return. Image editing hydrates originals and supporting variants into
that scratch directory. Shutdown removes it, so successful work needs no persistent
uploads volume and another replica can continue immediately.

This covers TypedPress uploads and WordPress attachment uploads through the standard
core/editor/REST APIs, image generation and image edit/restore. A plugin that writes
directly to disk, bypasses attachment hooks, stores a filesystem pathname as its
own durable record, or replaces upload/image hooks must integrate explicitly.
Unattached arbitrary filesystem uploads, plugin caches, themes and plugin installs
are outside this upload contract. This is not an interception layer for every PHP
filesystem write. Disable external image-CDN plugins when using this backend;
they own separate rewrite/offload contracts.

## Failures and recovery

S3 configuration never falls back to durable local bytes. A failed upload returns
an error. TypedPress's request transaction rolls back metadata, and new objects have
rollback compensation. Replacements use immutable object keys, so rollback keeps
the previous committed version. Deletions revoke database-backed download URLs at
commit and try provider deletion afterwards. Failed deletes do not resurrect rows.
Deletion and rollback compensation check live database references before removing
bytes, so a temporary metadata transition cannot delete a final manifest's objects.
Retirement also invalidates request-local reuse of those objects.
Provider details and signed requests are excluded from public errors and logs.

A DB-backed Action Scheduler action reconciles one page of at most 100 objects
against live file rows and attachment manifests. It only collects unreferenced
objects older than 24 hours, covering process crashes, rollback cleanup failure
and provider outages during deletion. Database/provider read errors fail the action;
they are never interpreted as an empty reference set. Pagination continues through
scheduled actions; hourly runs retry failures. Run Action Scheduler on a reliable
worker/cron in production. Give each app's requests a deadline below the 24-hour
cleanup grace. Keep the namespace option with database backups. For versioned S3
buckets, provider lifecycle rules must expire noncurrent versions/delete markers.

Core WordPress writes outside TypedPress's API retain core's own metadata/error lifecycle;
they are not silently wrapped in a new transaction model. Partially completed core
attachment operations can require ordinary WordPress metadata repair. The object
reconciler removes bytes only after their database references disappear.

## Existing data and configuration changes

This release does not migrate an existing uploads directory. Use S3 on a fresh
app, or perform a deliberate migration of local file rows and attachment manifests
before enabling it on an existing site. Reads of unmigrated local resources fail
with `uploads_migration_required`; no durable local read fallback is used and local
bytes are not silently deleted. Keep the existing backend until that migration is
verified. Changing the bucket, prefix, app identity or site namespace also requires
an explicit data migration. No migration history or existing SQL storage is rewritten
by this configuration option.

For local development, `uploads: { backend: "local" }` retains existing disk storage
and private-file web-server protection probes. Omitted configuration retains that
default. Selecting S3 bypasses local `.htaccess` probes; provider authorization and
private API grants protect its objects instead.

fields.title: npm compatibility
fields.description: Which npm packages compile to PHP.

record.body:
TypedPress compiles selected JavaScript and TypeScript package source into PHP. It does
not run Node.js on the server. Install dependencies with npm, then import the
qualified helpers from an ordinary TypedPress action.

`examples/npm-compat` compares pinned published packages under Node and freshly
compiled PHP. Each successful route runs the generated action, not just the
compiler. Its provenance file pins the original source SHA-256 and npm tarball
integrity; verification refuses changed source bytes even when the installed
package reports the right version.

The application example at `examples/npm-compat/app/typedpress.config.ts` builds a link
from user input with these unchanged published libraries:

| Package             | Qualified entry   | Use                                           | License |
|---------------------|-------------------|-----------------------------------------------|---------|
| url-join 5.0.0      | `lib/url-join.js` | Join URL paths, query fragments and protocols | MIT     |
| just-template 2.2.0 | `index.mjs`       | Interpolate text and nested properties        | MIT     |
| escape-html 1.0.3   | `index.js`        | Escape interpolated text and HTML attributes  | MIT     |

`just-template` does **not** escape HTML. The example explicitly escapes the
values before interpolation. It also preserves upstream's falsy-value behavior:
zero, false and missing values interpolate as empty strings.

From `examples/npm-compat`, with `typedpress` on PATH:

```sh
npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund
TP_BIN="$(command -v typedpress)" npm run verify -- --isolated
typedpress build app
typedpress dev app --port "$PORT"
```

Choose an unused local port and set `PORT` first. Send an anonymous request to
the website URL printed by `typedpress dev`:

```sh
curl "$SITE_URL/__tp/api/v1/actions/link" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"slug":"café & tea","title":"Tea & <scones>"}'
```

The action returns `/notes/caf%C3%A9%20%26%20tea` and an anchor containing
`Tea & <scones>`. WordPress owns the request, validation and application
state. The generated PHP action executes the library algorithms.

To verify in a separate npm installation without changing the example's shared
`node_modules`, set `NPM_COMPAT_NODE_MODULES` to that installation's absolute
`node_modules` path and use `--isolated`. Set `TP_WP_PLUGIN_CACHE` to a private
cache when running concurrent builds. Reports and generated projects live under
the printed temporary directory; `--only url-join --only just-template --only application-combined` selects the new library routes and their composition.

## Boundaries

The probes qualify selected exports and representative inputs. They do not
certify arbitrary npm packages, every export or every overload. Published ESM
source routes preserve the original bytes. CommonJS source routes replace only
the export assignment; typed routes add the explicitly recorded parameter
annotations. Temporary `@typedpress-npm-compat/*` packages are typed adapters, not
unchanged upstream packages. Declaration files are not automatically hydrated.
Package TypeScript sources compile through the same checked JavaScript domain
as `.js`: TypedPress erases their types instead of modelling them, so a package's
generic signatures, assertion functions, `this` types and symbol-keyed types no
longer block compilation. Authored code receives JavaScript values from them and
refines with `typeof`/`instanceof`.

Imported JavaScript can read the first-class array `slice` method. Borrowed
`Array.prototype.slice` supports dense arrays and ordinary `arguments`, including
`call`/`apply`, negative indexes, omitted/undefined end and null end. It snapshots
length before converting indexes and reads elements afterward. Arbitrary
array-like receivers and sparse results throw explicit TypeErrors. This is not
support for arbitrary prototype or host behavior. Authored TypeScript `unknown`
stays statically checked.

`ts-dedent` 2.3.0's published JavaScript passes the callable string probe; its
published TypeScript source passes that probe too. Repeated array/interpolation
calls still conservatively lose a captured string/nonempty proof and produce a
located `F4001` refusal in its interpolation callback. Tagged-template syntax
remains unsupported. No blanket array-index totality is assumed to bypass this.

`fuzzysearch` 1.0.3 remains unsupported: its unchanged source uses a labeled loop,
which produces a located `F1002` diagnostic. It is not a qualified dependency.
Custom object `toString` during authored `String(value)` conversion remains a
runtime limit. Browser/Node host APIs, asynchronous library effects, arbitrary
prototypes/accessors and package declaration hydration remain outside the
qualified subset.

The generated link action has also been exercised on a disposable WordPress
7.1.4 / PHP 8.5 / SQLite Database Integration 3.1.2 installation with the pinned
platform plugins. That checks real WordPress execution and cleanup; it does not
qualify MariaDB, Studio lifecycle, remote deployment or an external provider.

fields.title: Sealed mode
fields.description: A site where only the code the app lists runs.

record.body:
A site that runs only TypedPress's code can say so in its config:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  name: "shop",
  sealed: true,
  plugins: { "classic-editor": "1.6.7" },
});
```

With `sealed: true`, the only code that runs as a plugin is:

| Code                                                                                                                                                                                                    | Where it comes from                                                                  |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| TypedPress's own plugins: `typedpress-runtime`, `typedpress-identity`, TypedPress's admin `typedpress-admin` (whether or not the build ships it), and the app plugin `typedpress-app-<name>`            | shipped in the compiler and built from this project (`typedpress build`)             |
| the platform plugins TypedPress pins: Secure Custom Fields, Action Scheduler, MCP Adapter, Two Factor, and Polylang when the config sets `locales` ([wp-plugins.md](/docs/reference/wordpress-plugins)) | exact versions with checksums in TypedPress's release                                |
| the plugins the config declares under `plugins`                                                                                                                                                         | exact versions, with checksums in the committed `tp/_generated/wp-plugins.lock.json` |
| plugin packages under `use` (`definePlugin`)                                                                                                                                                            | compiled into the app plugin; see [below](#plugin-packages)                          |

Two plugins are never on the list, declared or not: `vip-block-data-api` and
`vip-decoupled-bundle`. The Block Data API answers a post's stored content
after an item-level check only, which shows a rich text field that one of the
app's field rules hides, and the decoupled bundle ships that API. `typedpress build`
refuses a sealed config that declares either, the site refuses to activate
either, and a host that enforces the list never loads either, even if a list
written some other way names them.

Sealed mode is off by default. With it off, activating other plugins stays
open, as WordPress ships it, and nothing below applies: no hook is added and no
build output changes.

`typedpress build` computes the list once, by plugin directory name, and writes the
same list everywhere it is read: `sealed.plugins` in the app's `schema.php` (what
the running app uses), and `sealed` in `typedpress-manifest.json`, in the hosted
manifest and in the build store's manifest (what a host uses). A hosted build
can't declare WordPress plugins at all, so its list is TypedPress's and the
platform's.

On the site, a plugin counts as listed when it is the main file of a listed
directory: `<slug>/<file>.php`. The site checks the directory name. Versions and
checksums are checked when the build fetches the plugin, not again on the site.

## What sealed mode guarantees, and where

WordPress 7.1 loads a request in this order (`wp-settings.php`):

1. drop-ins that load at start-up: `fatal-error-handler.php`, `maintenance.php`
   while the site is in maintenance, `advanced-cache.php` (with `WP_CACHE`),
   `db.php`, `object-cache.php`, and `sunrise.php` on multisite (with `SUNRISE`).
   The other drop-ins (`php-error.php`, `db-error.php`, `install.php` and the
   multisite `blog-*.php` pages) load only when their case arises;
1. must-use plugins (`wp-content/mu-plugins/*.php`);
1. network-active plugins, on multisite;
1. active plugins, in the order of the `active_plugins` option: TypedPress's app
   plugin is one of them;
1. the active theme's `functions.php`, then the rest of WordPress.

An ordinary plugin can't stop another plugin that WordPress has already loaded
in the same request, and the start-up drop-ins and every must-use plugin load
before any plugin. So what sealed mode guarantees depends on who loads TypedPress.

### On a plain WordPress host: refusals and a report

TypedPress is an active plugin there. While it is active, sealed mode:

- **refuses to activate** anything not on the list, for every user,
  administrators included: wp-admin's Plugins screen (one, bulk and network
  activation), core's REST plugins route (in every request form: `?rest_route=`,
  letter case, `_method`; `/batch/v1` doesn't take that route), and WP-CLI's
  `wp plugin activate`. All of them go through WordPress's `activate_plugin()`,
  which asks TypedPress before it loads the plugin. In wp-admin the Activate link is
  replaced by "Sealed: not in typedpress.config.ts". WP-CLI prints TypedPress's refusal,
  which names `typedpress.config.ts`; REST answers core's own 403
  (`rest_cannot_activate_plugin`).
- **refuses to deactivate, from wp-admin and REST, the plugins the app runs on**:
  TypedPress's own and the platform's. With the app stopped nothing would refuse
  anything, so this is what keeps an administrator from switching the list off
  in the browser. Declared plugins can be deactivated and reactivated freely.
- **reports** what is loaded, to administrators:
  - `plugins` and `networkPlugins`: active plugins that aren't on the list
    (one of the two never-listed plugins included). A plugin that was active
    before sealed mode turned on appears here and keeps running; TypedPress never
    deactivates or deletes anything.
  - `muPlugins`, `dropins`, `theme`: every must-use plugin, every drop-in
    present, and the active theme's PHP (see below). No config can list these,
    and a host's own are among them, so they are shown, not judged.
  - where: `GET /__tp/api/v1` under `runtime.wp.sealed` (`{enforced}` only for
    anyone who isn't an administrator); `typedpress doctor --site <url>`, whose
    `sealed` check fails when an unlisted plugin is active and which lists the
    rest for information (sign in with `typedpress login`, or `TP_APP_PASSWORD` / `TP_TOKEN`);
    and a wp-admin notice naming the unlisted active plugins.

This is not a guarantee that only listed code runs, and it holds only against
people working through WordPress. Someone with a shell is outside it:
`wp --skip-plugins` loads no plugin (TypedPress included) and can activate or
deactivate anything, as can writing the `active_plugins` option or the plugin
files directly. An unlisted plugin activated that way is reported on the next
request. A must-use plugin or drop-in placed on the server always loads.

### Where the host mounts TypedPress through the build store: enforced

A host that mounts TypedPress with the build store loader
(decision) runs its own code before
WordPress reads its plugin list, so it can enforce the list. In a must-use
plugin of the host's (or its `sunrise.php`), where `add_filter()` exists:

```php
require_once "$root/runtime/$revision/typedpress-loader.php";
use TypedPress\Loader\Loader;

$sealed = Loader::sealed($root, $build);   // null when the build isn't sealed
if ($sealed !== null) {
    define('TP_SEALED_ENFORCED', true);
    $filter = static fn ($active) => Loader::allowedPlugins((array) $active, $sealed);
    add_filter('option_active_plugins', $filter, PHP_INT_MAX);
    // WordPress writes the option back from what it read: keep the hidden entries stored.
    add_filter('pre_update_option_active_plugins', static function ($new) use ($filter, $sealed) {
        remove_filter('option_active_plugins', $filter, PHP_INT_MAX);
        $stored = (array) get_option('active_plugins', []);
        add_filter('option_active_plugins', $filter, PHP_INT_MAX);

        return Loader::keepUnlisted((array) $new, $stored, $sealed);
    }, PHP_INT_MAX);
}
Loader::load($root, $build, $options);
```

With that, an unlisted plugin that is active in the option doesn't load, and it
stays in the stored option: sealing a site hides it, and unsealing brings it
back. With `TP_SEALED_ENFORCED` defined, the report says `enforced: "host"`.
The report trusts that constant; it doesn't check the host's filter.

On multisite the same applies to the network's `active_sitewide_plugins` (its
keys are the plugin files). That option is shared by every site of the network,
so a host filters it per request with `site_option_active_sitewide_plugins` and
must not let a write from a sealed site's request drop other sites' entries.
TypedPress has no test on multisite; treat that part as the host's to verify.

The host also controls its own must-use plugins and drop-ins, so it ships only
what it needs there. The host contract states the list and
these calls. TypedPress writes nothing to `wp-config.php` or the must-use plugins
directory itself, and nothing changes for sites that don't serve a TypedPress app.

### Theme PHP

Switching themes isn't plugin activation, and sealed mode doesn't refuse it. A
block theme renders from templates, but WordPress still includes its
`functions.php` on every request and includes each PHP file in its `patterns/`
directory to register that pattern. The report names the active theme's
`functions.php` and the number of PHP pattern files, so the owner sees that
theme code runs. A classic theme's template files are PHP too and aren't
counted. TypedPress's own minimal block theme ships no PHP and is never reported.

## Plugin packages

Plugin packages (`use: [seo()]`) aren't WordPress plugins: the compiler turns
them into PHP inside the app plugin.

The compiler is their security boundary. TypedPress compiles a closed subset of
TypeScript and refuses everything else, so a plugin's compiled code can only
call the TypedPress APIs it names: there is no `eval`, no dynamic `require`, no file
or process access, and no reaching into PHP or WordPress except through the
`php/wordpress` functions the compiler records. The compiler records every
capability a plugin's code uses, including through its helpers and the npm
packages it imports: reads, writes and deletes per kind, hooks, actions,
outgoing hosts, environment variables, mail, jobs, timers, abilities, WordPress
hooks and PHP functions. `tp/_generated/plugins.lock.json` is the grant. With
`--frozen`, or when `CI` is set, a build whose plugin needs a capability the
lock doesn't hold fails; narrowing the lock by hand makes the compiler refuse
the code that exceeds it. A plugin can't import app modules or another plugin's
package, and its state is kept apart from every other plugin's
(decision).

The limits:

- **No resource limits.** A plugin runs in the same PHP process as the app, with
  no CPU or memory limit of its own. A throw in its hook rolls back the
  request's writes, as an app hook's does.
- **A grant is as wide as it reads.** A granted read plus a granted outgoing
  host can carry what was read to that host, or by mail with a mail grant.
  `typedpress check --json` reports the handlers that both read and send. That report
  works by handler; a hook that forwards the row it was handed isn't counted as
  a read. An `http` grant of `*` is any public host.
- **Granted PHP functions and abilities do what they do, within the guard.** A
  grant such as `php: wordpress:update_option` allows that function with any
  argument the guard below allows, and a granted ability runs another plugin's
  PHP. Read those lines of the lock as you would read the code.
- **A local build can widen the lock.** Without `--frozen` or `CI`, `typedpress build` adds a newly needed capability to the lock and prints the change;
  committing the lock is the approval. Build in CI (or with `--frozen`) so
  nothing is granted without a reviewed commit.

## The WordPress guard

App code and plugin packages reach WordPress only through `php/wordpress`, and
some of WordPress's settings would let that code past everything above: writing
`active_plugins`, `template` or `stylesheet` loads PHP already on disk without
going through `activate_plugin()`, and `users_can_register` with `default_role`
set to `administrator` makes every signup an administrator. So, sealed or not,
`get_option`, `update_option` and `delete_option` refuse the options listed in
`runtime/TypedPress/Wp/guard.json`, each with the
reason it is there:

- options that load code or pick what loads: `active_plugins`,
  `active_sitewide_plugins`, `recently_activated`, `uninstall_plugins`,
  `auto_update_plugins`, `auto_update_themes`, `template`, `stylesheet`,
  `template_root`, `stylesheet_root`, `current_theme`, `allowedthemes`, `WPLANG`,
  `cron`, `db_version`, `initial_db_version`, `jetpack_*` and transients
  (`_transient_*`, `_site_transient_*`, which hold the plugin update packages);
- options that move sign-in or mail: `siteurl`, `home`, `admin_email`,
  `new_admin_email`, `upload_path`, `upload_url_path`;
- options that decide roles: `users_can_register`, `default_role`,
  `{prefix}user_roles`, `site_admins`, `comment_registration`, and the pending
  confirmations a link applies: multisite invitations (`new_user_*`, which add
  the stored user with the stored role) and `adminhash`;
- options that route the site: `rewrite_rules`, `permalink_structure`,
  `show_on_front`, `page_on_front`, `page_for_posts`, `blog_public`,
  `fresh_site`;
- TypedPress's own `tp_*` options;
- options that hold secrets, which can't be read either: the salts and keys
  (`auth_key`, `secret_key`, ... `*_salt`), `recovery_keys`, `mailserver_pass`,
  and any name containing `secret`, `token`, `private`, `password`, `passwd`,
  `credential`, `api_key`, `apikey` or `access_key` (`jetpack_private_options`,
  `jetpack_secrets`).

Names compare as MySQL compares them: trimmed and case-insensitive, and a name
with any character outside printable ASCII is refused. A literal name fails the
build with `F4301`; a name built at runtime is refused with `403 protected_option` before WordPress sees the call. `wp_insert_post`, which
WordPress runs without a capability check, takes `post`, `page` or another
plugin's public post type only, so a published `customize_changeset` can't apply
settings and a TypedPress kind's post type can't skip its access rules. It takes only
the fields its type declares (`post_title`, `post_content`, ...): `ID`,
`import_id`, `meta_input`, `tax_input` and the rest are refused with `403 protected_post_field`, whatever the value's type said at build time, so it can't
overwrite an existing post.

The catalog admits no function that activates plugins, switches themes, or
changes roles, users, capabilities, user or post metadata, cron, or site
options (`add_option`, `update_site_option`, ...); `guard.json` lists them under
`neverAdmitted`, and a test fails if one is added to the catalog. An
`existingTable` can't bind
WordPress's, TypedPress's or Action Scheduler's tables or another site's.

## What else stays open

Sealed mode is about which code runs as a plugin. Content, media, users,
settings and each plugin's own settings stay as they are. Installing, updating
and deleting plugins from wp-admin are already refused on every TypedPress site
(the `pluginAndThemeInstalls` switch); translations still install, and a
translation file is PHP that WordPress includes.

fields.title: App services
fields.description: Search, mail and the other services an app gets from WordPress.

record.body:
TypedPress's native services module adds validated contact forms, queued mail, publication search and Stripe-hosted checkout. WordPress remains the authority for users, publication and content permissions. The existing TypedPress transaction, receipt, outbox and Action Scheduler implementations own atomic writes, request replay and delivery retries.

Author services in `typedpress.config.ts` or a trusted WordPress plugin. Both configure the same native runtime. TypeScript pages call the HTTP endpoints with `fetch`; no JavaScript service runtime is needed.

## Enable and configure

The runtime registers the services module, its built-in jobs and its system tables automatically. The TypeScript example configures the services at build time:

```ts
import { collection, defineConfig, env, text } from "typedpress";

const posts = collection({ title: text(), excerpt: text().optional() }, {
  title: "title", drafts: true, access: { read: "anyone" },
});

export default defineConfig({
  collections: { posts },
  services: {
    forms: {
      contact: {
        fields: {
          email: { type: "email", notNull: true, rules: { max: 191 } },
          message: { type: "text", notNull: true, rules: { min: 3, max: 2000 } },
        },
        recipient: env("APP_SERVICES_RECIPIENT"),
        sender: env("APP_SERVICES_SENDER"),
        limit: 5,
      },
    },
    search: { posts: ["title", "excerpt"] },
    products: { workshop: { name: "WordPress workshop", amount: 1900, currency: "usd" } },
    checkoutReturnUrl: "https://example.test/checkout",
  },
});
```

`recipient` and `sender` require `env("NAME")`. The compiler emits variable names into a private `tp_services_config` filter in the app's `functions.php`; it never reads their build-machine values. WordPress resolves them when the mail job runs. Services are excluded from `schema.php`, migration snapshots, generated client descriptors and the public schema. The provider and rate-limit variables below retain their native runtime names; they are deployment settings, not additional `services` options.

The compiler rejects unknown options, duplicate declarations and invalid definitions at their source property. Form fields support `text`, `email`, `integer` and `boolean`, optional `notNull`, and integer `rules.min`/`rules.max` for text length or integer bounds. Boolean fields have no bounds. Omit unused sections; a supplied registry or form field map must be nonempty. Form and product ids are lowercase slugs of at most 80 characters. Products require a nonempty name of at most 160 UTF-8 bytes, an integer amount from 50 to 99,999,999 and three lowercase currency letters. Configure `products` and an absolute HTTP(S) `checkoutReturnUrl` together.

Search keys name authored collections; the compiler binds them to the stored collection name. Each must enable `drafts: true` and list at least one authored text column (not the system `status`) without duplicates. HTTP queries use the stored name: the example above uses `posts`; the runnable example's `articles` key uses `storageName: "service_posts"`, so its request uses `collection=service_posts`. Runtime row and field access rules still apply.

Classic PHP plugins remain supported. The generated filter runs at priority 10 and merges `forms`, `search` and `products` by entry name. An authored entry replaces the whole same-name entry supplied by an earlier filter; unrelated entries and native options survive. A trusted filter at priority 20 can deliberately extend or override the result. Native plugins can use the runtime's broader schema validation features; the TypeScript bridge accepts only the documented subset.

For PHP authoring, a trusted WordPress plugin supplies private configuration through `tp_services_config`. The complete working example is typedpress-app-services.php. It defines:

- Form `contact`, with the existing schema column definitions for email and message validation.
- Searchable `posts` fields `title` and `excerpt`.
- Product `workshop`, priced at 1900 USD minor units on the server.
- An application-owned checkout return URL.

Recipients, senders and provider secrets are environment-variable names in this plugin. Values are resolved at runtime through `TypedPress\Env`, which also supports wp-config constants, except WordPress's own database login, keys and salts (see Runtime variables). They never enter generated schema, client JavaScript, catalog descriptions or responses.

| Variable                                             | Purpose                                                                             |
|------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `TP_SERVICES_RATE_SECRET`                            | Random deployment secret used to hash client addresses for rate counters            |
| `TP_SERVICES_MAIL_TO`, `TP_SERVICES_MAIL_FROM`       | One valid recipient and sender address each, as referenced by the example form      |
| `TP_SERVICES_SMTP_HOST`                              | Optional native SMTP transport; omit to use the existing WordPress mail integration |
| `TP_SERVICES_SMTP_PORT`                              | SMTP port, default 587                                                              |
| `TP_SERVICES_SMTP_ENCRYPTION`                        | PHPMailer encryption, default `tls`; empty only for a local sink                    |
| `TP_SERVICES_SMTP_USER`, `TP_SERVICES_SMTP_PASSWORD` | Optional SMTP authentication                                                        |
| `TP_SERVICES_STRIPE_SECRET`                          | Stripe API secret, supplied only on the server                                      |
| `TP_SERVICES_STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`                  | Signing secret for this endpoint's Stripe events                                    |

Keep prices, currency, product names and the return URL in trusted server configuration. Use HTTPS for the deployed site and return URL. Configure a real WP-Cron or WP-CLI cron runner for Action Scheduler on deployed WordPress.

## HTTP contract

Paths below follow `/__tp/api/v1`. Successes use `{ "data": ... }`; failures use the existing problem-document envelope. Both POST entry points require an `Idempotency-Key` header of 1–64 bytes. Retry the same intent with the same body and key; use a new key after editing the input.

| Method and path                                    | Input / result                                                                                                                               |
|----------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `POST /services/forms/contact`                     | `{ "website": "", "data": { "email": "visitor@example.test", "message": "Hello there" } }` → submission id and queued notification receipt |
| `GET /services/submissions/{id}`                   | Editor-only saved values plus job state, attempt count and completion time                                                                   |
| `GET /services/search?collection=posts&q=workshop` | At most 20 published, accessible results whose configured fields hold every word, with those fields                                          |
| `POST /services/checkout`                          | `{ "product": "workshop" }` → opaque status token, status path and `requested` state                                                       |
| `GET /services/checkout/{token}`                   | Current payment state, server price, checkout URL when available and checkout-job status                                                     |
| `POST /services/stripe/webhook`                    | Raw Stripe event body plus `Stripe-Signature`; authenticated receipt and duplicate indicator                                                 |

The checkout token is a bearer capability. Keep it in the browser session; do not publish it or attach it to analytics. Its hash is stored on the order. The existing HTTP replay receipt necessarily retains the original response, including this token, in server-only storage for its normal retention window.

## Forms and email

The supported form fields are text, email, integer and boolean. Schema validation rejects unknown fields and invalid values before any writes. Requests are limited to 32 KiB. A filled `website` honeypot is rejected. While Akismet has a key (the same rule as comments: Jetpack's connection or `WPCOM_API_KEY`), each submission is sent to Akismet's comment-check as a `contact-form` comment, modelled on Jetpack Forms' request: the first email field is the author's email, a `name` field the author, the other text the content, with the visitor's address, user agent and referrer. A submission Akismet calls spam is refused with `422 spam` and nothing but its receipt is written; it still uses a slot in the rate window, and a retry with the same `Idempotency-Key` gets the same answer without asking Akismet again. Unlike Jetpack Forms, a refused submission is not kept for review. An unreachable Akismet lets the submission through. Fixed fifteen-minute rate windows use durable counters on the app connection: five accepted intents per address/form by default, configurable from 1 to 100. Valid receipt replays do not consume another slot. Stale address counters expire after one day.

Only `REMOTE_ADDR` identifies the client. Forwarded headers are untrusted; configure the web server's trusted-proxy handling if it is behind a proxy. These controls reduce basic automated spam; they are not a CAPTCHA or a moderation service.

The submission and mail job commit together. An aborted transaction removes both, along with the job's Action Scheduler action and the replay receipt: the action is written in the same transaction. The native callable mail handler runs outside a database transaction. WordPress owns MIME and PHPMailer; without an SMTP override, existing WordPress mail plugins remain authoritative. Each send restores the mailer's previous message identity and any transport settings it overrides, including on failure.

Job states distinguish `pending`, `running`, `failed`, `dead` and `done`. A mail job becoming `done` means the configured transport accepted the message. It does not prove inbox placement. Delivery is at least once: a worker crash after SMTP acceptance can cause another attempt. The submission supplies a stable Message-ID, but SMTP offers no universal deduplication guarantee. Submissions and mail job inputs remain private; no public submission-status lookup is provided.

## Search and native content changes

Search is the same search as `posts.list({ search })` and `GET /search`, narrowed to the configured fields: a viewer-bound `db()->findMany` with `search` and `searchFields`, an explicit `published` filter, and the configured fields as the returned columns. A row matches when every word of `q` starts a word in one of those fields (search index). Existing row and field access rules run before SQL; asking for a configured field the caller may not read is a 403, so a hidden field is never a membership oracle. An editor's draft privileges do not make draft content searchable here.

The index is kept in step inside every write's transaction, wp-admin and core REST saves included. Editing, unpublishing, republishing or deleting through WordPress takes effect on the next query. Search is word-prefix matching in the kind's own order (oldest first here), not semantic search, fuzzy ranking or an external search provider. It supports publication-enabled TypedPress collections; configured fields must be authored text fields (not `status`), the fields the index holds.

## Hosted checkout and webhook recovery

Only a product id is accepted from the client. The order snapshots the name, integer minor-unit amount, currency, return URL and absolute expiry. No card fields, arbitrary checkout URLs or client prices are accepted. A job calls the fixed Stripe Checkout endpoint with pinned API version `2024-06-20`, an order-specific Stripe idempotency key and immutable request bytes. It runs after commit and outside the write transaction. Checkout sessions expire after one hour; creation retries stop once the original expiry is less than thirty minutes away. A lost response retries the same Stripe key inside that bounded window.

An intent whose creation window closes becomes `expired`; its job finishes without another provider request. The browser can start a fresh intent immediately. A concurrent signed payment state is preserved.

The returned URL must be HTTPS on `checkout.stripe.com`. The browser follows it; payment details go directly to Stripe. The return page does not mark an order paid. It refreshes the server's signed-event state using the saved browser-session token.

Stripe's raw-body timestamped v1 HMAC is checked within a five-minute tolerance before persistence. Session events must match the saved order id, session identity when known, currency, total amount and payment mode. Event ids and body hashes are stored in a durable payment-event ledger. Replays return the recorded acknowledgement; substitution under the same id is rejected. Event recording and order transitions share a transaction. Invalid events consume no ledger entry.

The lifecycle is `requested → ready → processing → failed/expired → paid`. Failed and expired sessions may still settle on a later authenticated success. `paid` is absorbing: late failure, expiry and unpaid-completion events cannot undo it. A webhook arriving before the checkout worker records the session is supported. The checkout worker never regresses an event-derived state.

The supported subset is one product, quantity one, one-off payment. Currency amount conventions must be checked for the currencies you configure. Subscriptions, tax, shipping, discounts, refunds, disputes, Connect and fulfillment integrations are outside this module. Fulfillment should use the saved paid state and a durable application operation, never the browser return URL.

## Run and verify

See the TypeScript example for the compiler-to-WordPress journey, and the PHP example for browser acceptance commands. `tests/services_config.rs` owns authoring validation and one compiled-plugin journey through real WordPress/SQLite and loopback SMTP. The existing PHP feature owner remains `tests/php/services_test.php`; it owns delivery retries, publication permissions and payment protocol behavior.

Local evidence proves WordPress 7.1.4, SQLite Database Integration 3.1.2, Action Scheduler 4.2.0 and WordPress's bundled PHPMailer 7.1.1. The example and runtime services are first-party code. No additional upstream SDK, plugin source or license notices were copied or removed. The existing WordPress and plugin licenses remain in their original owners.

The local SMTP sink proves the SMTP conversation and stored MIME bytes. Local signed Stripe protocol tests prove this runtime's validation, ledger, transitions and restart behavior. They are not Stripe sandbox acceptance or hosted mailbox delivery. Provider qualification requires designated test credentials and actual provider effects. Neither is claimed by the local suite. MySQL/MariaDB contention is also outside the SQLite evidence.

fields.title: WordPress plugin dependencies
fields.description: The WordPress plugins an app depends on, pinned in a lock file.

record.body:
Declare additional plugins in `typedpress.config.ts`. Rust fetches and validates their
archives during `typedpress build --target wp`; the deployed runtime stays PHP only.
`typedpress check` validates declarations and the dependency graph without network I/O.
Standalone builds validate the config but never acquire or emit these plugins.

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "typedpress";

export default defineConfig({
  name: "site",
  target: "wp",
  collections: {},
  plugins: {
    "classic-editor": "1.6.7",
  },
});
```

A runnable collection example is in `examples/wp-plugins/typedpress.config.ts`:

```sh
cargo run -- build examples/wp-plugins
```

Commit the generated `tp/_generated/wp-plugins.lock.json` with the config. For an exact
WordPress.org slug/version, the first successful build records the archive's
SHA-256; this first acquisition trusts the HTTPS response from WordPress.org.
Subsequent builds enforce that checksum even after deleting the download cache.
An authored `sha256` can pin the first acquisition too. Changing a version creates
a new pin; replacing bytes at the same source/version fails. To intentionally
repin that release, remove its lock entry and supply the new authored checksum.

Required platform plugins are supplied by TypedPress through the same resolver; users
need not list them. The current pins are SCF 6.9.7, Action Scheduler 4.2.0, MCP
Adapter 0.7.1 and Two Factor 0.17.0, plus Polylang 3.9 when `locales` is
configured. Users cannot remove them. Akismet isn't a platform plugin: spam
checks use the Akismet a site sets up through Jetpack, only while it has a key
(Jetpack's connection or `WPCOM_API_KEY`); it checks comments and Services
form submissions. Without one, neither is spam-checked and `typedpress doctor`
reports `spam checks: off`. Explicit overrides must satisfy the platform floor. `wp_plugins::version::at_least` owns comparison
using PHP `version_compare` ordering, including WordPress beta/RC/pl suffixes.
The exact header version is checked against the declaration; numeric trailing
zero differences are accepted (the Polylang 3.9 archive declares 3.9.0).

With `sealed: true`, the plugins declared here (and the platform pins) are the
only ones a site runs as plugins besides TypedPress's own; see [sealed mode](/docs/reference/sealed-mode).

## Supported plugins

TypedPress doesn't support every WordPress plugin. The plugins and version ranges the
TypedPress team tests are listed in
`src/wp_plugins/supported.json`: a minimum
version (inclusive) and an optional `below` bound (exclusive), compared with PHP
`version_compare`. The platform pins above are always on that list.

Any other plugin or version still installs. `typedpress check` and `typedpress build` print a
warning for it, and the wasm compiler returns the same text in
`unsupportedPlugins`:

```text
warning: plugin hello-dolly 1.7.2 is not supported by the TypedPress team. TypedPress installs it, but doesn't test it; TypedPress doesn't support every WordPress plugin. To ask for support, open an issue: https://github.com/spacefast/zero/issues
```

To get a plugin supported, open an issue with its slug, the version you need,
and what you use it for.

## Resources and explicit dependencies

The package key is the sole installation identity. An exact version string uses
WordPress.org. A detailed entry can supply the Blueprint v1 resource explicitly:

```ts
{
  plugins: {
    "classic-editor": {
      version: "1.6.7",
      pluginData: {
        resource: "wordpress.org/plugins",
        slug: "classic-editor.1.6.7.zip",
      },
    },
  },
}
```

An explicit archive reference must agree with the declaration's slug and version.
Plugins use top-level key/value entries and require exact versions. Floating
versions, ranges, tags such as `latest`, and different package identities are
rejected. Exact versions begin with a digit and may contain ASCII letters,
digits, dots, underscores, plus signs, and hyphens.

For a URL ZIP, supply `pluginData: { resource: "url", url: "https://…" }` and a
64-character lowercase hexadecimal `sha256`. URLs require HTTPS, except HTTP
loopback fixture servers; credentials and fragments are rejected. The package key is
the destination directory identity; `version` must match the plugin header.
For example, this URL declaration installs the same pinned public package:

```ts
plugins: {
  "classic-editor": {
    version: "1.6.7",
    pluginData: {
      resource: "url",
      url: "https://downloads.wordpress.org/plugin/classic-editor.1.6.7.zip",
    },
    sha256: "4b2b45b19c61f627ff8730222692a691023dea3435b35b8db95a2418b45ece65",
  },
}
```

The archive must contain one root directory or root-level plugin files, with one
root PHP `Plugin Name` header. Vendor wrappers with additional nested directories
must be repackaged. Original plugin license/readme files are preserved.

`requires: ["other-plugin"]` declares build dependencies by slug. Each dependency
must have its own exact package entry or be supplied by the platform. A plugin's
`Requires Plugins` header must be covered by this list. TypedPress neither guesses
versions nor fetches undeclared transitive packages. Duplicate declarations,
missing dependencies, cycles, and reserved `typedpress-*` identities fail. Metadata is
ordered by dependency, then lexically for independent nodes; this is also usable
as a deployment activation order, though the build never activates plugins.

## Output and failure behavior

WordPress builds use `tp/dist/wp-content` (`--out` selects
the content root), containing `plugins/<dependency>` alongside the generated app
plugin. Acquired ZIPs live in `.tp/cache/plugins/<sha256>.zip`; locked archives
can be reused offline. A corrupt cache entry fails rather than trusting or
silently replacing it. The cache is disposable; the project lock is not.

All downloads, extraction, header checks, and generated PHP lint finish in staging
before publishing output. Failed downloads, bad hashes, invalid archives, and
output collisions leave the previous output and project lock intact. Existing
unrelated plugins remain. Existing dependency destinations are replaced only if
the previous project lock owns their unchanged tree. Local changes and unmanaged
collisions fail with an error; remove or move the conflicting directory explicitly.
Removing a declaration does not uninstall its existing output directory.

Extraction rejects traversal/absolute paths, backslashes, control characters,
symlinks/special files, duplicate or case-colliding paths, file/directory conflicts,
and inconsistent local/central ZIP headers. Limits: 64 MiB downloaded, 256 MiB expanded, 20,000 ZIP entries,
60 seconds per acquisition, five redirects. Output trees containing symlinks or
special files are refused. Builds targeting the same project/output are serialized
by exclusive lock files; after a killed build, remove the named stale build lock
